rows.label: The process of assigning a standard scientific name
rows.explanation: Nomenclature supplies standard names so regional common names do not cause confusion.

rows.label: Determining which known organism a specimen represents
rows.explanation: Identification establishes the identity of a specimen by comparing its characters with known organisms.

rows.label: Grouping organisms using shared characters
rows.explanation: Classification organises diversity into groups that can be studied and compared.

rows.label: The study that explicitly incorporates evolutionary relationships into organismal diversity
rows.explanation: Systematics considers diversity together with relationships, including common ancestry.

rows.label: The Latin root of the term systematics
rows.explanation: Systema refers to systematic arrangement and is the root of systematics.

rows.label: The author of Systema Naturae
rows.explanation: Linnaeus used Systema Naturae as the title of his systematic work.

rows.label: The scientist associated with popularising binomial nomenclature
rows.explanation: Linnaeus established the widely adopted two-part naming convention.

rows.label: The number of principal components in a binomial
rows.explanation: A binomial contains the generic name and the specific epithet; an author citation is additional.

rows.label: The first component of Panthera leo
rows.explanation: Panthera is the genus and leo is the specific epithet.

rows.label: The second component of Homo sapiens
rows.explanation: Sapiens is the epithet; Homo sapiens together identifies the species.

rows.label: The appropriate initial letter for a generic name
rows.explanation: A generic name begins with a capital letter.

rows.label: The appropriate initial letter for a specific epithet
rows.explanation: The specific epithet starts with a small letter even when the genus is capitalised.

rows.label: The conventional typeface for a printed binomial
rows.explanation: Printed generic names and specific epithets are conventionally italicised.

rows.label: The treatment of the two words of a handwritten binomial
wrong: Join both words without a space
rows.explanation: Separate underlining substitutes for italics in handwritten scientific names.

rows.label: The language form generally used for scientific biological names
rows.explanation: Names follow Latin form even when derived from another language.

rows.label: The role of Linn. in Mangifera indica Linn.
rows.explanation: Linn. credits Linnaeus as the describing author rather than adding a species-name component.

rows.label: The usual position of an author citation
rows.explanation: The author's abbreviated name follows the binomial.

rows.label: The code concerned with animal nomenclature
rows.explanation: The International Code of Zoological Nomenclature governs zoological names.

rows.label: The code abbreviation used by the NCERT chapter for botanical nomenclature
rows.explanation: The chapter uses ICBN for botanical naming rules; this question asks specifically for the textbook abbreviation.

rows.label: The main reason common names are unreliable for global scientific communication
rows.correct: They vary across languages and regions
rows.explanation: The same organism may have different common names in different places.

rows.label: The taxonomic rank represented by a group of related genera
rows.explanation: A family brings together related genera and is above genus.

rows.label: The taxonomic rank represented by a group of related families
rows.explanation: Related families are grouped into orders.

rows.label: The taxonomic rank represented by a group of related orders
rows.explanation: A class contains related orders.

rows.label: The taxonomic rank represented by a group of related animal classes
rows.explanation: Animal classes with broad shared features are placed in a phylum.

rows.label: The plant rank conventionally equivalent to phylum
rows.explanation: Division is the botanical term traditionally used at the phylum level.

rows.label: The highest rank in the seven-rank hierarchy used in this chapter
rows.explanation: Among species, genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom, kingdom is the broadest.

rows.label: The rank immediately below family
rows.explanation: The descending sequence is order, family, genus, species.

rows.label: The rank immediately below order
rows.explanation: Families are contained within orders.

rows.label: The rank immediately below class
rows.explanation: Orders subdivide a class.

rows.label: The rank immediately below kingdom in the conventional animal hierarchy
rows.explanation: A kingdom contains phyla, which in turn contain classes.

rows.label: The collective arrangement of successive taxonomic ranks
rows.explanation: The hierarchy orders categories from species to kingdom.

rows.label: The plural of taxon
rows.explanation: Taxa is the standard plural form of taxon.

rows.label: The distinction between Mammalia and class
rows.correct: Mammalia is a taxon at the rank of class
wrong: Mammalia is a genus and class is a species
Class is a specimen and Mammalia is an organ
rows.explanation: Class names the rank; Mammalia names one biological group occupying it.

rows.label: The general change in shared characters when moving from species to kingdom
wrong: They become identical at every rank
rows.explanation: Broader categories include more diverse organisms and therefore fewer common characters.

rows.label: The general change in inclusiveness when moving from kingdom to species
rows.explanation: Lower ranks contain narrower sets of organisms.

rows.label: The lowest common rank necessarily shared by two species in the same genus
rows.explanation: Different congeneric species share genus and all higher ranks but not species.

rows.label: The most specific rank necessarily shared by two genera in the same family
rows.explanation: Distinct genera can share a family without belonging to the same genus.

rows.label: The inference justified when two organisms belong to different families of one order
rows.correct: They share that order and its higher ranks
rows.explanation: Membership of one order implies membership of its class, phylum and kingdom.

rows.label: The inference justified by membership of the same species
rows.correct: The organisms also share genus and family
wrong: The organisms must have different genera
The organisms must have different families
No higher category can be inferred
rows.explanation: In a consistent hierarchy, members of a species share all its higher categories.

rows.label: The inference not justified by membership of one family
rows.correct: The organisms must belong to the same species
rows.explanation: A family may contain many genera and many species.

rows.label: The genus of humans
rows.explanation: The human binomial is Homo sapiens.

rows.label: The family of humans in the chapter's classification table
rows.explanation: Homo is placed in Hominidae.

rows.label: The order of humans in the chapter's classification table
rows.explanation: The table uses Primata for the human order, commonly called Primates.

rows.label: The class of humans
rows.explanation: Humans are mammals and belong to Mammalia.

rows.label: The phylum of humans
rows.explanation: Humans are vertebrate chordates.

rows.label: The scientific name of the housefly
rows.explanation: The familiar housefly is identified by the binomial Musca domestica.

rows.label: The genus of the housefly
rows.explanation: Musca is the generic component of Musca domestica.

rows.label: The family of the housefly
rows.explanation: Musca is grouped within Muscidae.

rows.label: The order of the housefly
rows.explanation: Houseflies belong to the two-winged insect order Diptera.

rows.label: The class of the housefly
rows.explanation: The housefly is an insect, not a vertebrate.

rows.label: The phylum of the housefly
rows.explanation: Insects are arthropods with jointed appendages and an exoskeleton.

rows.label: The scientific name of bread wheat
rows.explanation: Triticum aestivum names bread wheat.

rows.label: The genus of bread wheat
rows.explanation: Triticum is wheat's genus; the other options are higher taxa.

rows.label: The family of wheat
rows.explanation: Wheat belongs to the grass family Poaceae.

rows.label: The order assigned to wheat in the NCERT example table
rows.explanation: The table groups wheat in Poales above Poaceae.

rows.label: The class assigned to wheat in the NCERT example table
rows.explanation: Wheat is a monocotyledonous angiosperm.

rows.label: The scientific name of mango
rows.explanation: Mangifera indica is the mango binomial.

rows.label: The family of mango
rows.explanation: Mango is placed in Anacardiaceae.

rows.label: The order assigned to mango in the NCERT example table
rows.explanation: The chapter's table assigns mango to Sapindales.

rows.label: The class assigned to mango in the NCERT example table
rows.explanation: The table uses the traditional dicot class for mango.

rows.label: The lowest shared category of mango and wheat in the chapter's example table
rows.explanation: The table assigns them different classes but the same angiosperm division.

rows.label: The genus shared by lion, tiger and leopard
rows.explanation: Panthera leo, Panthera tigris and Panthera pardus share the generic name.

rows.label: The family shared by Panthera and Felis
rows.explanation: Both genera are cats and are placed in Felidae.

rows.label: The order shared by Felidae and Canidae
rows.explanation: Cats and dogs belong to different families within Carnivora.

rows.label: The genus shared by potato and brinjal in the chapter's examples
rows.explanation: Solanum tuberosum and Solanum melongena are examples of congeneric species.

rows.label: The specific epithet in Solanum tuberosum
rows.explanation: The second word tuberosum is the specific epithet and begins with a lowercase letter.

rows.label: The family containing Solanum, Petunia and Datura
rows.explanation: These distinct genera share the family Solanaceae.

rows.label: The class shared by the human and the lion
rows.explanation: Humans and lions belong to different orders but both are mammals.

rows.label: The number of pairs of legs characteristically used to recognise adult insects
rows.explanation: Six legs arranged in three pairs are a characteristic insect feature.

rows.label: The minimum evidence needed to place an unknown specimen in a taxonomic group
wrong: The colour of its storage box
rows.explanation: Taxonomic placement depends on relevant biological characters rather than arbitrary labels.

rows.label: The study input that extends taxonomy beyond outward appearance
rows.explanation: Modern taxonomy uses cellular, internal, developmental and ecological information.

rows.label: The early basis of many human classifications of organisms
rows.correct: Use for food, clothing or shelter
rows.explanation: Practical human needs motivated early grouping of organisms.

rows.label: The biological species concept's key criterion for natural populations
rows.correct: Interbreeding with reproductive isolation from other groups
rows.explanation: The biological species concept emphasises gene exchange within a species and isolation between species.

rows.label: A limitation of applying the biological species concept directly
rows.correct: It is difficult to test for fossils and asexual organisms
wrong: It requires all organisms to be plants
It defines species solely by size
rows.explanation: Breeding cannot be observed in fossils and is not applicable in the same way to asexual lineages.

rows.label: The scientist prominently associated with the biological species concept
rows.explanation: Mayr developed and promoted the biological species concept.

rows.label: The appropriate conclusion when two binomials share only the epithet indica
rows.correct: Their genera must still be checked
wrong: They must be varieties of mango
rows.explanation: An epithet alone does not uniquely identify a species across genera.

rows.label: The correct interpretation of Panthera leo and Panthera tigris
wrong: One family name and one order name
rows.explanation: Their common first word indicates a shared genus; their epithets distinguish species.

rows.label: The correct interpretation of Solanum and Solanaceae
rows.explanation: Solanum is nested in the family Solanaceae.

rows.label: The best reason a genus name alone is insufficient to specify a species
rows.correct: A genus may include several species
wrong: A genus is always an individual
A genus has no taxonomic meaning
A genus is always a kingdom
rows.explanation: A specific epithet is needed because the genus can contain multiple species.

rows.label: The rank with the greatest similarity among its members in the conventional hierarchy
rows.explanation: The lowest principal category groups organisms sharing the most detailed similarities.

rows.label: The meaning of biodiversity at the organismal level discussed in this chapter
wrong: Number of rocks in a habitat
rows.explanation: Biodiversity includes the variety of organisms rather than abiotic conditions alone.

rows.label: The appropriate handling of an unfamiliar organism before assigning it a name
wrong: Choose any unused common word immediately
rows.explanation: Reliable naming depends on knowing which organism the name represents.

rows.label: The relation between species and a specimen
rows.correct: A specimen is an individual representative; species is a taxonomic group
wrong: A species is always one preserved individual
Specimen is a rank above kingdom
Species and specimen are interchangeable ranks
rows.explanation: Many individual specimens can represent one species.

rows.label: The effect of adding a newly recognised species to an existing genus
wrong: The genus automatically becomes a kingdom
rows.explanation: Recognising a species changes genus membership without automatically changing higher ranks.

rows.label: The appropriate inference from similar appearance alone
rows.correct: Additional characters may be needed for identification
wrong: The organisms must be one species
rows.explanation: Superficial similarity is useful but may not establish identity or reproductive compatibility.

rows.label: The principal function of a taxonomic key
rows.explanation: Keys lead a user through contrasting diagnostic traits to an identification.

rows.label: A paired set of alternatives in a dichotomous key
rows.explanation: A dichotomous key presents two contrasting choices as a couplet.

rows.label: An individual alternative within a taxonomic key couplet
rows.explanation: Each statement offered as one choice in a couplet is called a lead.

rows.label: The resource designed to maintain living plant collections for study
rows.explanation: A botanical garden cultivates labelled living plants.

rows.label: The useful information on a herbarium label
rows.correct: Collection locality, date and scientific identification
wrong: Only the price of the paper
Only the colour of the folder
rows.explanation: Collection data and identification connect a preserved specimen to its origin and taxonomic identity.

rows.label: The proposer of the five-kingdom classification
rows.explanation: Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom scheme in 1969.

rows.label: The year of Whittaker's five-kingdom proposal
rows.explanation: The five-kingdom system was proposed in 1969.

rows.label: The kingdom containing prokaryotes in Whittaker's system
rows.explanation: Monera groups organisms lacking a membrane-bound nucleus.

rows.label: The kingdom primarily used for unicellular eukaryotes in this framework
rows.explanation: Protista contains diverse single-celled eukaryotic organisms in the textbook system.

rows.label: The kingdom separated from plants mainly because its members absorb organic nutrients
rows.explanation: Fungi are heterotrophic absorbers rather than photosynthetic plants.

rows.label: The major criterion distinguishing Monera from Protista
rows.explanation: Nuclear organisation separates prokaryotic Monera from eukaryotic Protista.

rows.label: The major nutritional mode typical of Animalia
rows.explanation: Animals typically ingest food and digest it internally.

rows.label: The principal nutritional mode of green plants
rows.explanation: Green plants use light energy to synthesise organic food.

rows.label: The structural feature shared by plants, fungi and most bacteria
rows.explanation: Cell walls occur in all three groups, whereas bacteria lack membrane-bound organelles.

rows.label: The classification approach based on evolutionary relationships
rows.explanation: Phylogeny traces descent and common ancestry.

rows.label: The bacterial shape described as coccus
rows.explanation: Cocci are spherical bacteria.

rows.label: The bacterial shape described as bacillus
rows.explanation: Bacilli have an elongated rod form.

rows.label: The bacterial shape described as vibrio
rows.explanation: Vibrios are curved, comma-shaped bacteria.

rows.label: The bacterial shape described as spirillum
rows.explanation: Spirilla have a spiral form.

rows.label: The archaebacteria associated with highly saline habitats
rows.explanation: Halophilic archaea tolerate very high salt concentrations.

rows.label: The archaebacteria associated with hot, acidic habitats
rows.explanation: Thermoacidophiles are adapted to heat and acidity.

rows.label: The archaebacteria associated with methane generation
rows.explanation: Methanogens generate methane during anaerobic metabolism.

rows.label: The digestive chamber of cattle commonly associated with methanogens
rows.explanation: The anaerobic rumen supports methanogenic archaea.

rows.label: The photosynthetic pigment shared by cyanobacteria and green plants
rows.explanation: Cyanobacteria carry out oxygenic photosynthesis using chlorophyll a.

rows.label: The specialised nitrogen-fixing cell in Nostoc
rows.explanation: Heterocysts provide conditions suitable for nitrogen fixation.

rows.label: An example of a filamentous cyanobacterium
rows.explanation: Anabaena is a filamentous cyanobacterium that can contain heterocysts.

rows.label: The energy source for chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria
rows.explanation: These bacteria use energy from inorganic oxidation to synthesise organic compounds.

rows.label: The common bacterial mode of multiplication
rows.explanation: Bacteria usually divide into two daughter cells by fission.

rows.label: The bacterial group lacking a cell wall
rows.explanation: Mycoplasmas lack the rigid wall present in most bacteria.

rows.label: The expected effect of a drug acting only on bacterial wall synthesis on Mycoplasma
rows.explanation: A wall-specific target is absent in wall-less Mycoplasma.

rows.label: The classification of cyanobacteria in the five-kingdom scheme
rows.correct: Monera despite the name blue-green algae
rows.explanation: Cyanobacteria are prokaryotic and therefore placed in Monera.

rows.label: The shell material characteristic of diatom frustules
rows.explanation: Silica impregnates the two overlapping parts of a diatom wall.

rows.label: The arrangement of the two halves of a diatom wall
rows.correct: One fits over the other like a box and lid
wrong: One forms a root and the other a shoot
rows.explanation: Diatom frustules have two overlapping halves.

rows.label: The textbook group containing diatoms and golden algae
rows.explanation: Chrysophytes include diatoms and desmids in the chapter's classification.

rows.label: The ecological role of many marine diatoms
rows.explanation: Photosynthetic diatoms contribute substantially to aquatic primary production.

rows.label: The common external covering of dinoflagellates described in NCERT
wrong: A silica box in every species
rows.explanation: Many dinoflagellates have stiff cellulose plates on the surface.

rows.label: The usual flagellar arrangement of dinoflagellates
rows.explanation: Two differently oriented flagella produce their characteristic movement.

rows.label: The dinoflagellate cited as a red-tide example
rows.explanation: Rapid multiplication of Gonyaulax can colour seawater and release harmful toxins.

rows.label: The flexible outer covering of Euglena
rows.explanation: Euglenoids have a protein-rich pellicle instead of a rigid cell wall.

rows.label: The nutritional response of Euglena when light is unavailable
wrong: It must fix nitrogen in a heterocyst
rows.explanation: Euglenoids can switch from photosynthetic to heterotrophic nutrition depending on conditions.

rows.label: The habitat commonly associated with euglenoids in the textbook
rows.explanation: Many euglenoids occur in stagnant freshwater.

rows.label: The feeding stage formed by aggregating slime moulds
rows.explanation: The slime-mould plasmodium is a spreading feeding mass, distinct from the malarial genus Plasmodium.

rows.label: The structures produced by slime moulds under unfavourable conditions
rows.explanation: Resistant spores help slime moulds survive adverse conditions.

rows.label: The locomotory and feeding extensions of Amoeba
rows.explanation: Amoeba extends cytoplasm as pseudopodia for movement and engulfing prey.

rows.label: The protozoan associated with sleeping sickness
rows.explanation: Trypanosoma is a parasitic flagellated protozoan.

rows.label: The locomotory structures of Paramecium
rows.explanation: Numerous coordinated cilia move Paramecium and direct food towards its gullet.

rows.label: The protozoan group to which the malarial parasite belongs in NCERT
rows.explanation: Plasmodium is treated as a sporozoan in the textbook scheme.

rows.label: An amoeboid protozoan genus containing parasitic species
rows.explanation: Entamoeba includes intestinal parasites such as E. histolytica.

rows.label: The collective name for a network of fungal filaments
rows.explanation: Interwoven hyphae form a mycelium.

rows.label: An individual thread-like fungal filament
rows.explanation: A hypha is a filament forming part of a fungal body.

rows.label: The description of fungal hyphae without cross walls and with many nuclei
rows.explanation: A coenocytic hypha contains multinucleate cytoplasm without regular septa.

rows.label: The fungal mode of feeding on dead organic material
rows.explanation: Saprotrophic fungi secrete enzymes and absorb dissolved products from dead substrates.

rows.label: The association of fungal hyphae with plant roots
rows.explanation: Mycorrhiza is a root-fungus association involving nutrient exchange.

rows.label: The fusion of fungal cytoplasm during sexual reproduction
rows.explanation: Plasmogamy joins the cytoplasm before or independently of nuclear fusion.

rows.label: The fusion of compatible fungal nuclei
rows.explanation: Karyogamy combines haploid nuclei to form a diploid nucleus.

rows.label: The nuclear condition denoted n + n in fungi
rows.explanation: A dikaryon has two unfused haploid nuclei rather than one diploid nucleus.

rows.label: The process restoring haploidy after fungal karyogamy
rows.explanation: Meiosis reduces chromosome number after the diploid stage.

rows.label: The mycelium typical of textbook Phycomycetes
rows.explanation: Phycomycetes are described as having coenocytic, aseptate hyphae.

rows.label: The site of asexual spore production in Rhizopus
rows.explanation: Rhizopus forms asexual spores inside sporangia.

rows.label: The motile asexual spores described for Phycomycetes
rows.explanation: Zoospores are motile, unlike nonmotile aplanospores.

rows.label: The nonmotile asexual spores described for Phycomycetes
rows.explanation: Aplanospores lack motility.

rows.label: The fungus-like organism placed among Phycomycetes in the NCERT framework and causing white rust
rows.explanation: NCERT groups Albugo with Phycomycetes; modern taxonomy places oomycetes separately from true fungi.

rows.label: The common name for Ascomycetes
rows.explanation: Their sexual spores develop in sac-like asci.

rows.label: The sac in which ascospores develop
rows.explanation: An ascus contains the sexually produced ascospores.

rows.label: The common exogenous asexual spores of Ascomycetes
rows.explanation: Conidia develop externally on specialised hyphae called conidiophores.

rows.label: The fruiting body containing asci
rows.explanation: Asci may be organised in fruiting bodies called ascocarps.

rows.label: The yeast used in bread and alcoholic fermentation
rows.explanation: Saccharomyces is a unicellular ascomycete used in fermentation.

rows.label: The ascomycete often used in genetic and biochemical research
rows.explanation: Neurospora has been a valuable experimental organism in genetics.

rows.label: The group containing morels and truffles in the textbook
rows.explanation: Morels and truffles are edible examples of sac fungi.

rows.label: The sexual spore-bearing structure characteristic of Basidiomycetes
rows.explanation: Karyogamy and meiosis occur in the basidium, which bears basidiospores externally.

rows.label: The usual number of basidiospores formed on a basidium in the textbook account
rows.explanation: Four haploid basidiospores are typically produced externally after meiosis.

rows.label: The fruiting body of a typical mushroom
rows.explanation: The visible mushroom is a basidiocarp bearing basidia.

rows.label: The genus associated with wheat rust
rows.explanation: Puccinia is a rust fungus placed in Basidiomycetes.

rows.label: The genus associated with smut disease
rows.explanation: Ustilago is a basidiomycete causing smuts.

rows.label: The familiar mushroom genus in NCERT examples
rows.explanation: Agaricus is a mushroom-forming basidiomycete.

rows.label: The textbook group called imperfect fungi
rows.explanation: This historical grouping contained fungi whose sexual stages were not known.

rows.label: The basis for moving a fungus out of Deuteromycetes in the textbook scheme
rows.explanation: An identified sexual stage permits placement in the appropriate sexual group.

rows.label: An example placed in Deuteromycetes by the chapter
rows.explanation: The textbook lists Alternaria among imperfect fungi.

rows.label: The photosynthetic partner of a lichen
rows.explanation: The phycobiont produces organic food by photosynthesis.

rows.label: The fungal partner of a lichen
rows.explanation: The mycobiont supplies a protective framework and helps obtain water and minerals.

rows.label: The reason lichens are useful pollution indicators
rows.correct: Many are sensitive to air pollution
wrong: All require sulphur dioxide to grow
rows.explanation: Lichen sensitivity can indicate air-quality deterioration.

rows.label: The material making up a viral capsid
rows.explanation: The capsid is a protein covering around the viral genome.

rows.label: The subunits composing a capsid
rows.explanation: Capsomeres assemble into the viral protein coat.

rows.label: The type of genome in tobacco mosaic virus
wrong: Both DNA and RNA as its genome
rows.explanation: TMV is an RNA virus.

rows.label: The hosts attacked by bacteriophages
rows.explanation: A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria.

rows.label: The condition required for multiplication of viruses
rows.explanation: Viruses depend on host machinery for replication.

rows.label: The scientist who demonstrated crystallisation of tobacco mosaic virus
rows.explanation: Stanley showed that viral material could be crystallised.

rows.label: The researcher associated with the phrase contagium vivum fluidum
rows.explanation: Beijerinck used this expression while studying the tobacco mosaic agent.

rows.label: The scientist associated with discovering viroids
rows.explanation: Diener identified the smaller infectious RNA agent causing potato spindle tuber disease.

rows.label: The disease used as the classic viroid example
rows.explanation: Potato spindle tuber disease is caused by a viroid.

rows.label: The infectious material in a prion
rows.explanation: Prions transmit a misfolded protein state without a nucleic-acid genome.

rows.label: The human disease classically associated with prions
rows.explanation: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease is a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy associated with prions.

rows.label: The reason viruses are not assigned an ordinary cellular kingdom in Whittaker's scheme
wrong: They contain a complete independent metabolism
rows.explanation: The kingdom scheme classifies cellular organisms; viruses lack cellular organisation.

rows.label: The main nutritional distinction between fungi and animals
wrong: Fungi ingest while animals absorb only through hyphae
Both always oxidise inorganic nitrogen for energy
rows.explanation: Fungi generally digest externally and absorb, whereas animals typically ingest food.

rows.label: The structure absent from a typical bacterium but present in a protist
rows.explanation: Prokaryotes have DNA but no membrane-bound nucleus.

rows.label: The approach using only a few superficial traits for grouping plants
rows.explanation: Artificial systems may use a small selection of traits that do not reliably reflect overall affinity.

rows.label: The approach considering many external and internal plant characters together
rows.explanation: Natural systems seek overall relationships using numerous characters.

rows.label: The classification approach centred on common ancestry
rows.explanation: Phylogenetic systems aim to reflect evolutionary descent.

rows.label: The taxonomic approach using chromosome number, structure and behaviour
rows.explanation: Cytotaxonomy draws evidence from cytological features, especially chromosomes.

rows.label: The taxonomic approach using chemical constituents of plants
rows.explanation: Chemotaxonomy uses biochemical patterns as evidence of relationships.

rows.label: The approach coding many characters for computer-assisted comparison
rows.explanation: Numerical taxonomy assigns codes to characters for quantitative comparisons.

rows.label: The pair associated with a natural system of flowering-plant classification
rows.explanation: Bentham and Hooker developed an influential natural system.

rows.label: The plant group containing Chlamydomonas, Volvox and Spirogyra
rows.explanation: All three are examples of green algae.

rows.label: The green alga with a colonial habit
rows.explanation: Volvox consists of a coordinated colony of cells.

rows.label: The green alga characteristically represented as a single motile cell
rows.explanation: Chlamydomonas is commonly a unicellular flagellated green alga.

rows.label: The green alga with spiral chloroplasts
rows.explanation: Spirogyra has ribbon-like chloroplasts arranged in spirals.

rows.label: The main chlorophyll combination in green algae
wrong: Chlorophyll b and c without a
rows.explanation: Green algae characteristically possess chlorophylls a and b.

rows.label: The chief storage carbohydrate in green algae
rows.explanation: Green algae store starch, often associated with pyrenoids.

rows.label: The chloroplast structures associated with starch formation in many green algae
rows.explanation: Pyrenoids are protein-rich chloroplast bodies surrounded by starch in many green algae.

rows.label: The typical inner wall layer of green algae in the NCERT description
rows.explanation: The wall commonly has an inner cellulose layer and an outer pectose layer.

rows.label: The pigment chiefly responsible for brown colour in brown algae
rows.explanation: Fucoxanthin masks the green colour of chlorophyll in brown algae.

rows.label: The chlorophyll combination characteristic of brown algae
rows.explanation: Phaeophyceae possess chlorophylls a and c with fucoxanthin.

rows.label: The principal stored food pair in brown algae
rows.explanation: Brown algae characteristically store laminarin and mannitol.

rows.label: The mucilaginous outer wall material of brown algae
rows.explanation: Algin forms part of the gelatinous covering of brown algal walls.

rows.label: The anchoring structure of a large brown alga
rows.explanation: A holdfast attaches the thallus without being a true root.

rows.label: The stem-like part of a large brown algal thallus
rows.explanation: The stipe supports the blade-like portion of the algal body.

rows.label: The leaf-like photosynthetic part of a large brown alga
rows.explanation: The expanded blade or frond is part of a thallus, not a true leaf with vascular tissue.

rows.label: The common flagellar pattern of motile brown algal cells
wrong: Two equal apical flagella in every species
Numerous cilia over the entire surface
rows.explanation: Brown algal motile cells typically carry two unequal laterally attached flagella.

rows.label: The brown alga represented by giant kelp-like forms
rows.explanation: Laminaria is a large marine brown alga.

rows.label: The group containing Ectocarpus, Fucus and Sargassum
rows.explanation: These genera are standard examples of brown algae.

rows.label: The pigment largely responsible for red colour in red algae
rows.explanation: Phycoerythrin gives many red algae their characteristic colour.

rows.label: The storage carbohydrate of red algae
rows.explanation: Floridean starch resembles amylopectin and glycogen structurally.

rows.label: The flagellar condition in the life cycle of red algae
wrong: All gametes have two equal flagella
rows.explanation: Red algae lack flagellated reproductive stages.

rows.label: The usual form of sexual reproduction in red algae
wrong: Conjugation by identical motile gametes only
rows.explanation: Red algae show oogamous reproduction with nonmotile gametes.

rows.label: The pair of red algal genera commonly used to obtain agar
rows.explanation: Agar from these red algae is used in culture media and food products.

rows.label: The red algal hydrocolloid commonly used as a thickener
rows.explanation: Carrageenan is obtained from red algae; algin is associated with brown algae.

rows.label: The edible red algal genus in the textbook examples
rows.explanation: Porphyra is a red alga consumed as food.

rows.label: The protein-rich unicellular alga used as a food supplement
rows.explanation: Chlorella is a unicellular green alga cultivated for protein-rich biomass.

rows.label: The fusion of gametes that are similar in size and form
rows.explanation: Isogamy involves morphologically similar gametes.

rows.label: The fusion of two gametes differing in size, without the strict egg-sperm condition
rows.explanation: Anisogamy involves unequal gametes; oogamy is a specialised unequal-gamete condition.

rows.label: The fusion of a large nonmotile egg with a smaller male gamete
rows.explanation: Oogamy differentiates a large egg and a smaller male gamete.

rows.label: The vegetative reproductive process in which algal body pieces grow into new individuals
rows.explanation: Each viable fragment may develop into a complete thallus.

rows.label: The motile asexual spores commonly produced by algae
rows.explanation: Zoospores move by flagella and germinate into new algal individuals.

rows.label: The reason bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom
rows.correct: They live on land but require water for fertilisation
wrong: They have both flowers and cones
rows.explanation: Motile male gametes require water to reach the egg.

rows.label: The structures anchoring a bryophyte gametophyte
rows.explanation: Bryophytes lack true roots and use rhizoids for anchorage.

rows.label: The vascular tissue condition of bryophytes
rows.correct: True xylem and phloem are absent
wrong: A vascular cambium surrounds every rhizoid
rows.explanation: Bryophytes are nonvascular land plants.

rows.label: The male sex organ of a bryophyte
rows.explanation: Antheridia produce the male gametes.

rows.label: The female sex organ of a bryophyte
rows.explanation: An archegonium contains the egg.

rows.label: The generation produced by a bryophyte zygote
rows.explanation: The diploid zygote develops into a multicellular sporophyte.

rows.label: The nutritional relation of a bryophyte sporophyte to its gametophyte
wrong: It always becomes an independent tree
rows.explanation: Bryophyte sporophytes retain nutritional dependence on the gametophyte.

rows.label: The division producing spores in a bryophyte capsule
rows.explanation: Diploid spore mother cells undergo meiosis to produce haploid spores.

rows.label: The liverwort bearing gemma cups
rows.explanation: Marchantia forms gemma cups on its thallus.

rows.label: The asexual buds produced within Marchantia gemma cups
rows.explanation: Gemmae detach and develop into new gametophytes.

rows.label: The usual rhizoid type in liverworts
wrong: Multicellular and branched in all cases
rows.explanation: Liverwort rhizoids are usually unicellular, unlike those of mosses.

rows.label: The rhizoid type of the leafy moss stage
rows.explanation: Moss leafy shoots are anchored by multicellular branched rhizoids.

rows.label: The source of the leafy moss shoot
rows.correct: A lateral bud on secondary protonema
rows.explanation: The leafy gametophyte develops as a bud from the protonemal system.

rows.label: The part of a moss sporophyte bearing spores
rows.explanation: Spore mother cells and spores develop within the capsule.

rows.label: The stalk connecting the foot and capsule in a moss sporophyte
rows.explanation: The seta elevates the moss capsule.

rows.label: The moss associated with peat formation
rows.explanation: Accumulated Sphagnum contributes to peat deposits.

rows.label: The feature making Sphagnum useful for packing living plant material
rows.explanation: Sphagnum retains moisture and can help protect living materials in transport.

rows.label: The principal plant body of a fern
rows.explanation: A fern's conspicuous plant is its vascular diploid sporophyte.

rows.label: The small gametophyte of a typical homosporous fern
rows.explanation: A fern spore commonly develops into a small free-living prothallus.

rows.label: The structures on a pteridophyte sporophyte that bear sporangia
rows.explanation: Sporophylls are modified leaves associated with sporangia.

rows.label: The compact aggregation of sporophylls in Equisetum
rows.explanation: Sporophylls may be organised in a cone-like strobilus.

rows.label: The pteridophyte group containing horsetails
rows.explanation: Equisetum is placed in Sphenopsida in the textbook scheme.

rows.label: The representative genus of Psilopsida in NCERT
rows.explanation: Psilotum represents Psilopsida in the chapter's classification.

rows.label: The textbook pteridophyte class containing Selaginella and Lycopodium
rows.explanation: Both genera are assigned to Lycopsida.

rows.label: The textbook class containing Pteris, Adiantum and Dryopteris
rows.explanation: These fern genera represent Pteropsida.

rows.label: The pteridophyte with small microphyllous leaves in NCERT examples
rows.explanation: Selaginella bears microphylls, unlike the larger leaves of ferns.

rows.label: The pteridophyte pair illustrating heterospory
rows.explanation: These genera produce microspores and megaspores.

rows.label: The gametophyte that develops from a microspore in a heterosporous plant
rows.explanation: Microspores give rise to male gametophytes.

rows.label: The gametophyte that develops from a megaspore
rows.explanation: Megaspores develop into female gametophytes.

rows.label: The condition in a plant producing only one kind of spore
rows.explanation: Homosporous plants do not distinguish microspores from megaspores.

rows.label: The evolutionary significance of retaining the female gametophyte in heterosporous plants
rows.correct: A step toward the seed habit
wrong: The origin of a bacterial wall
The origin of red algal pigments
rows.explanation: Retention protects fertilisation and embryo development, anticipating aspects of seeds.

rows.label: The major reproductive distinction between gymnosperms and angiosperms
rows.correct: Gymnosperm ovules are not enclosed by an ovary
rows.explanation: Angiosperm ovules are inside an ovary, whereas gymnosperm ovules remain exposed.

rows.label: The gymnosperm genus with mycorrhizal roots in the textbook
rows.explanation: Pinus roots commonly associate with fungi as mycorrhizae.

rows.label: The gymnosperm genus with coralloid roots
rows.explanation: Cycas coralloid roots harbour nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

rows.label: The symbiotic organisms in Cycas coralloid roots
rows.explanation: The cyanobacterial partners can fix atmospheric nitrogen.

rows.label: The gymnosperm with a typically unbranched main stem in NCERT
rows.explanation: Cycas is contrasted with the branched stems of Pinus and Cedrus.

rows.label: The gymnosperm commonly cited among the tallest trees
rows.explanation: Giant redwoods belonging to Sequoia are exceptionally tall gymnosperms.

rows.label: The leaf form that reduces exposed surface area in conifers
rows.explanation: Narrow needle leaves help reduce water loss in conifers.

rows.label: The stomatal adaptation helping many conifers conserve water
rows.explanation: Sunken stomata and a thick cuticle help reduce transpiration.

rows.label: The spore condition of gymnosperms
rows.explanation: Gymnosperms produce both microspores and megaspores.

rows.label: The reduced male gametophyte of a gymnosperm
rows.explanation: The microspore develops into a highly reduced pollen-bearing male gametophyte.

rows.label: The sporangium associated with the gymnosperm ovule
rows.explanation: The ovule contains the megasporangium or nucellus surrounded by an integument.

rows.label: The tissue of a gymnosperm ovule enclosing the megaspore mother cell
rows.explanation: The nucellus is the megasporangial tissue within the ovule.

rows.label: The division producing megaspores from a megaspore mother cell
rows.explanation: A diploid megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form haploid megaspores.

rows.label: The typical fate of three of the four gymnosperm megaspores
rows.explanation: Usually one functional megaspore forms the female gametophyte.

rows.label: The gymnosperm with male and female cones on the same tree in the textbook
rows.explanation: Pinus is monoecious, bearing both male and female reproductive structures on one plant.

rows.label: The gymnosperm with male and female reproductive structures on separate plants
rows.explanation: Cycas is dioecious; male and female plants are distinct.

rows.label: The usual agent transferring gymnosperm pollen to exposed ovules
rows.explanation: Wind-borne pollen reaches the ovule; a pollen tube subsequently delivers male gametes.

rows.label: The angiosperm structure that encloses ovules before fertilisation
rows.explanation: The ovary contains the ovules and develops into a fruit after fertilisation.

rows.label: The usual product of an angiosperm ovule after fertilisation
rows.explanation: A fertilised ovule develops into a seed, while the ovary forms the fruit.

rows.label: The usual product of an angiosperm ovary after fertilisation
rows.explanation: The ovary matures into the fruit surrounding the seeds.

rows.label: The number of cotyledons characteristic of a monocot embryo
rows.explanation: Monocotyledons have one seed leaf; dicotyledons typically have two.

rows.label: The level of organisation characteristic of sponges
rows.explanation: Sponge cells show division of labour without organisation into true tissues.

rows.label: The level of organisation characteristic of cnidarians
rows.explanation: Cnidarians have cells organised into tissues.

rows.label: The symmetry permitting equal left and right halves in only one plane
rows.explanation: Bilateral symmetry has one principal plane of division.

rows.label: The symmetry typical of most adult sponges
rows.explanation: Most sponges cannot be divided into matching halves through a regular plane.

rows.label: The embryonic layer between ectoderm and endoderm in triploblastic animals
rows.explanation: Mesoderm is a true germ layer; mesoglea is not its equivalent.

rows.label: The body cavity completely lined by mesoderm
rows.explanation: A true coelom has a mesodermal lining on both body-wall and gut sides.

rows.label: The coelomic condition of flatworms
wrong: Haemocoel as the only defining feature
rows.explanation: Flatworms lack a cavity between the gut and body wall.

rows.label: The pattern of repeated body segments illustrated by an earthworm
rows.explanation: Metamerism involves serial repetition of body units and some organs.

rows.label: The number of openings in a complete digestive tract
rows.explanation: A complete tract has a separate mouth and anus.

rows.label: The circulatory arrangement in which haemolymph directly bathes tissues
rows.explanation: In open systems fluid leaves vessels and enters tissue spaces.

rows.label: The small pores admitting water into a sponge
rows.explanation: Water enters through ostia and passes through the canal system.

rows.label: The large opening through which water exits a sponge
rows.explanation: The osculum discharges water from the sponge's canal system.

rows.label: The collar cells driving water flow and trapping food in sponges
rows.explanation: Flagellated choanocytes generate currents and capture food particles.

rows.label: The principal type of digestion in sponges
rows.explanation: Sponge cells ingest and digest food internally.

rows.label: The freshwater sponge among the following genera
rows.explanation: Spongilla is a standard freshwater sponge example.

rows.label: The materials forming the supporting skeleton of sponges
rows.explanation: Sponges may have mineral spicules, proteinaceous spongin, or both.

rows.label: The stinging capsule within a cnidocyte
rows.explanation: A nematocyst discharges a thread used in prey capture and defence.

rows.label: The sessile cylindrical body form of a cnidarian
rows.explanation: Polyps such as Hydra usually remain attached to a substrate.

rows.label: The free-swimming umbrella-shaped form of a cnidarian
rows.explanation: Aurelia illustrates the medusoid body form.

rows.label: The alternation of polyp and medusa illustrated by Obelia
rows.explanation: Obelia alternates asexual polyp reproduction with the sexual medusa stage.

rows.label: The principal mineral of a stony coral skeleton
rows.explanation: Reef-forming corals deposit calcium carbonate skeletons.

rows.label: The cnidarian commonly called Portuguese man-of-war
rows.explanation: Physalia is a colonial cnidarian rather than a true fish.

rows.label: The locomotory structures of ctenophores
rows.correct: Eight rows of ciliated comb plates
rows.explanation: Coordinated beating of comb plates moves ctenophores through water.

rows.label: The habitat restriction of ctenophores in the textbook account
rows.explanation: Comb jellies are marine animals.

rows.label: The ctenophore genus among these examples
rows.explanation: Pleurobrachia is a comb jelly; Physalia is a cnidarian.

rows.label: The organs of osmoregulation and excretion in flatworms
rows.explanation: Flame cells form part of protonephridial systems.

rows.label: The flatworm renowned for regeneration
rows.explanation: Planarians can regenerate missing body regions from fragments.

rows.label: The genus commonly called tapeworm
rows.explanation: Taenia is an endoparasitic cestode or tapeworm.

rows.label: The genus commonly called liver fluke
rows.explanation: Fasciola is a parasitic flatworm associated with the liver and bile ducts.

rows.label: The main function of hooks and suckers in parasitic flatworms
rows.explanation: Attachment structures prevent displacement within the host.

rows.label: The digestive tract condition typical of roundworms
wrong: Radially branched with no anus in every species
rows.explanation: Roundworms have an alimentary canal with two openings.

rows.label: The sexual organisation typical of Ascaris
wrong: Each adult produces eggs and sperm
Only female individuals in every population
rows.explanation: Ascaris is dioecious and shows sexual dimorphism.

rows.label: The usual relative size of female and male Ascaris
rows.explanation: Female Ascaris generally have a larger body than males.

rows.label: The nematode genus associated with lymphatic filariasis
rows.explanation: Wuchereria can infect lymphatic vessels and cause elephantiasis.

rows.label: The roundworm commonly known as hookworm
rows.explanation: Ancylostoma attaches to the intestinal mucosa and feeds on blood.

rows.label: The excretory structures characteristic of annelids
rows.explanation: Annelid nephridia remove wastes and regulate fluid balance.

rows.label: The circulatory system generally described for annelids
wrong: Identical to a sponge canal system
rows.explanation: Blood circulates within vessels in the typical annelid system.

rows.label: The lateral swimming appendages of Nereis
rows.explanation: Parapodia are paired lateral outgrowths used in locomotion.

rows.label: The annelid genus commonly called a leech
rows.explanation: Hirudinaria is a leech with an annelid segmented body.

rows.label: The annelid with separate sexes among these textbook examples
rows.explanation: Nereis is dioecious, whereas earthworms and many leeches are hermaphroditic.

rows.label: The largest animal phylum by number of described species
rows.explanation: Arthropods, especially insects, account for the greatest described animal diversity.

rows.label: The main structural polysaccharide of the arthropod exoskeleton
rows.explanation: A chitin-containing cuticle forms the arthropod exoskeleton.

rows.label: The excretory tubules typical of insects
rows.explanation: Malpighian tubules remove wastes from haemolymph into the gut.

rows.label: The respiratory organs characteristic of a terrestrial insect
rows.explanation: A branching tracheal network delivers gases directly to tissues.

rows.label: The arthropod commonly called a living fossil in NCERT
rows.explanation: The horseshoe crab Limulus is cited as a living fossil.

rows.label: The insect genus used in commercial silk production
rows.explanation: Bombyx mori larvae produce silk cocoons.

rows.label: The second largest animal phylum in the textbook account
rows.explanation: Molluscs rank after arthropods in described species diversity in this account.

rows.label: The molluscan fold covering the visceral mass
rows.explanation: The mantle covers the visceral mass and commonly secretes the shell.

rows.label: The rasping feeding organ found in most molluscs
rows.explanation: The radula bears rows of teeth; bivalves are an important exception.

rows.label: The molluscan genus commonly called devil fish
rows.explanation: Octopus is a cephalopod mollusc, not a fish.

rows.label: The mollusc associated with pearl production
rows.explanation: Pearl oysters of Pinctada can deposit nacre around an irritant.

rows.label: The mollusc commonly called sea hare
rows.explanation: Aplysia is a gastropod mollusc.

rows.label: The body symmetry of an adult starfish
rows.explanation: Adult echinoderms are radially organised, commonly around five sectors.

rows.label: The body symmetry of a typical echinoderm larva
rows.explanation: Echinoderm larvae are bilateral even though adults are radial.

rows.label: The skeletal material of echinoderm ossicles
rows.explanation: Calcareous ossicles form the echinoderm endoskeleton.

rows.label: The locomotory extensions operated by the water vascular system
rows.explanation: Hydraulically operated tube feet participate in locomotion and other functions.

rows.label: The echinoderm commonly called brittle star
rows.explanation: Ophiura has slender flexible arms characteristic of brittle stars.

rows.label: The habitat of all living echinoderms
rows.explanation: Echinoderms are exclusively marine.

rows.label: The three body regions of Balanoglossus
rows.explanation: Hemichordates have a proboscis-collar-trunk body plan.

rows.label: The excretory structure described for hemichordates
rows.explanation: The proboscis gland participates in excretion in hemichordates.

rows.label: The embryonic origin of the notochord
rows.explanation: The notochord is a mesodermal supporting rod.

rows.label: The nerve cord arrangement characteristic of chordates
rows.explanation: A dorsal hollow neural tube is a key chordate feature.

rows.label: The restriction of the notochord in Urochordata
wrong: Throughout the adult body in every species
rows.explanation: Tunicate larvae have a tail notochord that is lost during metamorphosis in typical forms.

rows.label: The notochord condition in Cephalochordata
rows.correct: Extends from head to tail throughout life
wrong: Occurs only in a larval tail
Replaced completely by bone before hatching
rows.explanation: Branchiostoma retains a longitudinal notochord as an adult.

rows.label: The representative cephalochordate genus
rows.explanation: Branchiostoma, also called Amphioxus, is a lancelet.

rows.label: The mouth of a cyclostome
rows.explanation: Cyclostomes have a circular sucking mouth without jaws.

rows.label: The skeleton characteristic of Chondrichthyes
rows.explanation: Cartilaginous fishes have a cartilage-based endoskeleton.

rows.label: The scale type characteristic of sharks
rows.explanation: Placoid scales are tooth-like dermal structures.

rows.label: The buoyancy organ generally absent in cartilaginous fishes
rows.explanation: Sharks lack the air bladder present in many bony fishes.

rows.label: The flap covering the gills in most bony fishes
rows.explanation: An operculum covers the gill chamber in most Osteichthyes.

rows.label: The number of chambers in a typical fish heart
rows.explanation: A fish heart has one atrium and one ventricle.

rows.label: The bony fish commonly called seahorse
rows.explanation: Hippocampus is a marine bony fish.

rows.label: The cartilaginous fish commonly called electric ray
rows.explanation: Torpedo possesses electric organs.

rows.label: The number of heart chambers typical of amphibians
rows.explanation: Amphibians generally have two atria and one ventricle.

rows.label: The usual skin covering of amphibians
rows.explanation: Amphibian skin is usually moist and involved in gas exchange.

rows.label: The class containing Salamandra and Ichthyophis
rows.explanation: Salamanders and limbless caecilians are amphibians.

rows.label: The skin covering typical of reptiles
rows.explanation: Keratinised scales help reptiles limit water loss.

rows.label: The reptile group with a four-chambered heart
rows.explanation: Crocodilians have four heart chambers, unlike the usual textbook reptilian pattern.

rows.label: The reptile commonly called garden lizard
rows.explanation: Calotes is the garden lizard.

rows.label: The poisonous snake genus commonly called krait
rows.explanation: Bungarus includes kraits, which are venomous snakes.

rows.label: The skeletal feature helping reduce body mass in many birds
rows.explanation: Air spaces within many bones reduce mass while preserving support.

rows.label: The forelimb modification characteristic of birds
rows.explanation: Bird forelimbs are modified as wings, even in species unable to fly.

rows.label: The number of chambers in a bird's heart
rows.explanation: Two atria and two ventricles separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

rows.label: The temperature-regulation category shared by birds and mammals
rows.explanation: Birds and mammals produce substantial metabolic heat and regulate body temperature.

rows.label: The flightless bird genus Struthio
rows.explanation: Struthio is the ostrich.

rows.label: The gland defining the mammalian feeding adaptation for young
rows.explanation: Mammary glands secrete milk to nourish offspring.

rows.label: The muscular partition between thorax and abdomen in mammals
rows.explanation: The diaphragm separates body cavities and assists ventilation.

rows.label: The egg-laying mammal among these genera
rows.explanation: The platypus is an oviparous monotreme.

rows.label: The mammal genus commonly called flying fox
rows.explanation: Pteropus is a fruit bat capable of powered flight.

rows.label: The mammal genus commonly called kangaroo
rows.explanation: Macropus is a marsupial mammal.

rows.label: The embryonic structure giving rise to the primary root
rows.explanation: The radicle elongates into the primary root during germination.

rows.label: The root system characteristic of mustard
rows.explanation: The primary root persists and gives off lateral branches in mustard.

rows.label: The root system characteristic of wheat
rows.explanation: Roots arising near the stem base replace the short-lived primary root in wheat.

rows.label: Roots arising from plant parts other than the radicle
rows.explanation: Adventitious roots may arise from stems, nodes or leaves.

rows.label: The protective structure covering the growing root apex
rows.explanation: The root cap protects delicate apical cells as the root pushes through soil.

rows.label: The root region with actively dividing cells
rows.explanation: The apical meristem supplies new cells for root growth.

rows.label: The root region chiefly responsible for increase in length through cell enlargement
rows.explanation: Cells enlarge rapidly in the elongation zone behind the meristem.

rows.label: The root zone commonly bearing root hairs
rows.explanation: Differentiated epidermal cells develop root hairs in the maturation zone.

rows.label: The main function of root hairs
wrong: Conduct photosynthesis as the main organ
rows.explanation: Root hairs enlarge contact with soil water and dissolved minerals.

rows.label: The root modification storing food in carrot
rows.explanation: Carrot's swollen taproot stores reserve nutrients.

rows.label: The food-storing root of sweet potato
rows.explanation: Sweet potato stores food in swollen adventitious roots, unlike potato stem tubers.

rows.label: The supporting roots arising from lower stem nodes of maize
rows.explanation: Maize stilt roots grow obliquely from lower nodes into the soil.

rows.label: The upward-growing respiratory roots in Rhizophora
rows.explanation: Pneumatophores help gas exchange in waterlogged, oxygen-poor soil.

rows.label: The embryonic structure developing into the shoot
rows.explanation: The plumule forms the young shoot system.

rows.label: The point on a stem where a leaf arises
rows.explanation: Nodes are the sites of leaf and often bud attachment.

rows.label: The stem region between successive nodes
rows.explanation: Internodes separate adjacent nodes.

rows.label: The bud found in the angle between a leaf and stem
rows.explanation: An axillary bud occurs in the leaf axil and may form a branch or flower.

rows.label: The diagnostic feature identifying potato as a stem tuber
wrong: Presence of root hairs on each eye
rows.explanation: Potato eyes are nodes with buds, indicating stem origin.

rows.label: The underground stem modification of ginger
rows.explanation: Ginger is a horizontal underground stem with nodes, buds and scale leaves.

rows.label: The storage structure of onion
rows.explanation: An onion bulb has a short stem surrounded by fleshy leaf bases.

rows.label: The climbing stem modification of grapevine
rows.explanation: Grapevine tendrils are stem-derived climbing structures.

rows.label: The protective stem modification of Citrus
rows.explanation: Citrus thorns are modified axillary shoots.

rows.label: The flattened photosynthetic stem of Opuntia
rows.explanation: Opuntia stems conduct photosynthesis while leaves are reduced to spines.

rows.label: The underground condensed stem of Colocasia
rows.explanation: A corm is a short swollen underground stem.

rows.label: The horizontal creeping stem rooting at nodes in lawn grass
rows.explanation: Runners spread along the surface and establish new plants at nodes.

rows.label: The one-internode vegetative propagule characteristic of Pistia
rows.explanation: An offset is a short lateral branch typical of some floating aquatic plants.

rows.label: The leaf part attaching it to the stem
rows.explanation: The leaf base joins the leaf to the stem.

rows.label: The stalk of a typical petiolate leaf
rows.explanation: A petiole connects the lamina with the leaf base.

rows.label: The expanded blade of a leaf
rows.explanation: The lamina is the main flattened photosynthetic region.

rows.label: The swollen leaf base common in legumes
rows.explanation: A pulvinus is a swollen leaf base often involved in leaf movements.

rows.label: The small lateral appendages at the leaf base in a stipulate leaf
rows.explanation: Stipules flank the leaf base; not all leaves possess them.

rows.label: The net-like arrangement of veins in a leaf
rows.explanation: Reticulate veins form an interconnected network.

rows.label: The venation commonly found in grass leaves
rows.explanation: Monocot grasses commonly have veins running broadly parallel.

rows.label: The leaf type in which incisions reach the midrib and separate leaflets
rows.explanation: Deep incisions separating individual leaflets produce a compound leaf.

rows.label: The feature usually present at the base of a whole leaf but absent at leaflet bases
rows.explanation: An axillary bud distinguishes a leaf from an individual leaflet.

rows.label: The compound leaf type of neem
rows.explanation: Neem leaflets are arranged along a common rachis.

rows.label: The compound leaf type of silk cotton
rows.explanation: Silk cotton leaflets radiate from one point.

rows.label: The common axis bearing leaflets in a pinnate leaf
rows.explanation: The rachis is the extended leaf axis carrying leaflets.

rows.label: The arrangement with one leaf at each node
rows.explanation: Alternate leaves arise singly at successive nodes.

rows.label: The arrangement with two leaves at each node
wrong: Whorled with three or more leaves
rows.explanation: Opposite leaves occur in pairs at a node.

rows.label: The arrangement with more than two leaves at a node
rows.explanation: A whorl contains three or more leaves around the same node.

rows.label: The leaf arrangement illustrated by Alstonia
rows.explanation: Alstonia commonly bears a whorl of leaves at each node.

rows.label: The leaf arrangement illustrated by guava
rows.explanation: Guava leaves are arranged in opposite pairs.

rows.label: The climbing modification of pea leaflets
rows.explanation: Pea leaflets may be modified into tendrils for support.

rows.label: The main protective leaf modification in cactus
rows.explanation: Cactus leaves are reduced to spines, limiting water loss and providing defence.

rows.label: The photosynthetic flattened petiole of Australian Acacia
rows.explanation: A phyllode is a modified petiole, whereas a phylloclade is stem-derived.

rows.label: The insect-trapping modification of Nepenthes
rows.explanation: The pitcher is derived from the leaf and traps small animals.

rows.label: The arrangement of flowers on a floral axis
rows.explanation: Inflorescence describes the pattern of flowers on the reproductive axis.

rows.label: The inflorescence with an indefinitely growing main axis
rows.explanation: In racemose inflorescences the main axis continues growth.

rows.label: The inflorescence whose main axis ends in a flower
rows.explanation: A terminal flower limits main-axis growth in a cyme.

rows.label: The usual sequence of flower age along a racemose axis
rows.explanation: Acropetal succession places younger flowers toward the apex.

rows.label: The usual sequence of flower age in a simple cyme
rows.correct: Older terminal, younger toward the base
rows.explanation: Basipetal succession follows termination of the main axis by an older flower.

rows.label: The stalk of an individual flower
rows.explanation: The pedicel supports an individual flower.

rows.label: The swollen floral axis bearing the floral whorls
rows.explanation: Floral organs arise on the thalamus or receptacle.

rows.label: The outermost floral whorl in a typical complete flower
rows.explanation: The calyx consists of sepals outside the petals.

rows.label: The floral whorl made of petals
rows.explanation: Petals collectively form the corolla.

rows.label: The male reproductive whorl of a flower
rows.explanation: The androecium consists of stamens.

rows.label: The female reproductive whorl of a flower
rows.explanation: The gynoecium is composed of one or more carpels.

rows.label: The symmetry of a flower divisible into similar halves in many vertical planes
rows.explanation: Actinomorphic flowers show radial symmetry about their central axis.

rows.label: The symmetry of a pea flower
rows.explanation: A pea flower can be divided into equivalent halves in one principal vertical plane.

rows.label: The symmetry of a Canna flower
rows.explanation: Canna flowers cannot be divided into two equal halves by a vertical plane.

rows.label: A flower containing both stamens and carpels
rows.explanation: A bisexual flower has both male and female reproductive organs.

rows.label: A flower subtended by a bract
rows.explanation: Bracteate means a bract occurs at the base of the flower or its stalk.

rows.label: The condition in which sepals are fused
rows.explanation: Gamosepalous refers to union among sepals.

rows.label: The condition in which petals are free
rows.explanation: Polypetalous flowers have separate petals.

rows.label: The aestivation in which each petal overlaps the next in one direction
rows.explanation: Twisted aestivation produces regular overlap in a consistent direction.

rows.label: The aestivation with irregular petal overlap and no fixed direction
rows.explanation: Imbricate petals overlap irregularly.

rows.label: The aestivation characteristic of pea
rows.explanation: The standard overlaps the wings, which overlap the keel petals.

rows.label: The large posterior petal of a papilionaceous corolla
rows.explanation: The standard or vexillum is the largest petal in the pea-type corolla.

rows.label: The ovary position in an epigynous flower
rows.explanation: Other floral parts arise above the ovary in epigynous flowers.

rows.label: The stalk of a stamen
rows.explanation: The filament supports the pollen-bearing anther.

rows.label: The pollen-producing part of a stamen
rows.explanation: Pollen develops in the microsporangia of the anther.

rows.label: The attachment of stamens to petals
rows.explanation: Epipetalous stamens are attached to petals, as in brinjal.

rows.label: The condition with staminal filaments united into one bundle
rows.explanation: Monadelphous filaments form one bundle, as in China rose.

rows.label: The condition with staminal filaments united into two bundles
rows.explanation: Pea shows two bundles, commonly a 9+1 arrangement.

rows.label: The sterile stamen of a flower
rows.explanation: A staminode is a nonfunctional or sterile stamen.

rows.label: The pollen-receptive part of a carpel
rows.explanation: The stigma receives pollen during pollination.

rows.label: The slender connection between stigma and ovary
rows.explanation: The style connects the stigma to the ovary.

rows.label: The gynoecium with free carpels
rows.explanation: Apocarpous carpels remain separate, as in lotus.

rows.label: The gynoecium with fused carpels
rows.explanation: Carpels are united in a syncarpous gynoecium, as in tomato.

rows.label: The placentation of pea
rows.explanation: Ovules occur along the ventral suture of the single carpel.

rows.label: The placentation of tomato
rows.explanation: Ovules attach to a central axis in a multilocular ovary.

rows.label: The placentation of mustard
rows.explanation: Ovules arise from the inner ovary wall; a false septum may divide the chamber.

rows.label: The placentation of Dianthus
rows.explanation: Ovules attach to a free central axis without septa dividing the ovary.

rows.label: The placentation of sunflower
rows.explanation: The ovule is attached near the base of the unilocular ovary.

rows.label: The fruit wall formed from the ovary wall
rows.explanation: The pericarp may differentiate into outer, middle and inner layers.

rows.label: The hard stony inner layer of a mango fruit
rows.explanation: The lignified endocarp surrounds the seed in a drupe.

rows.label: The seed attachment scar
rows.explanation: The hilum marks the former attachment of the funicle.

rows.label: The small pore in a seed coat
rows.explanation: The micropyle permits water and gas entry during germination.

rows.label: The shield-shaped cotyledon of a grass embryo
rows.explanation: The scutellum is the single cotyledon of the grass embryo.

rows.label: The tissue responsible for continuing cell division in growing plant regions
rows.explanation: Meristematic cells retain the ability to divide and generate new tissues.

rows.label: The meristem located at the growing tips of roots and shoots
rows.explanation: Apical meristems drive primary growth at the ends of plant axes.

rows.label: The meristem commonly responsible for regrowth at the base of grass leaves
rows.explanation: Intercalary meristems remain between mature tissues and support renewed elongation.

rows.label: The meristem mainly associated with increase in girth
rows.explanation: Vascular and cork cambia add tissues laterally, increasing thickness.

rows.label: The type of growth primarily increasing root and shoot length
rows.explanation: Primary growth is mainly produced by apical and intercalary meristems.

rows.label: The cytoplasmic condition typical of active meristematic cells
rows.explanation: Actively dividing cells typically have dense cytoplasm and prominent nuclei.

rows.label: The vacuolar condition typical of young meristematic cells
rows.correct: Small vacuoles or no large central vacuole
wrong: One huge vacuole filling the entire cell
rows.explanation: Meristematic cells lack the large central vacuole typical of many mature plant cells.

rows.label: The tissue composed mainly of one type of cell
rows.explanation: Simple permanent tissues contain structurally similar cells performing related functions.

rows.label: The tissue composed of different cell types working together
rows.explanation: Xylem and phloem are complex tissues with multiple component cell types.

rows.label: The process by which meristem-derived cells become specialised
rows.explanation: Differentiation changes structure and function as cells mature.

rows.label: The simple tissue usually made of living thin-walled cells
rows.explanation: Parenchyma commonly has living cells with cellulose-rich primary walls.

rows.label: The main function of storage parenchyma
rows.explanation: Parenchyma stores starch, oils and other substances in many organs.

rows.label: The name for photosynthetic parenchyma containing chloroplasts
rows.explanation: Chlorenchyma specialises in photosynthesis.

rows.label: The parenchyma with large air spaces in many aquatic plants
rows.explanation: Aerenchyma facilitates internal gas movement and buoyancy.

rows.label: The tissue providing flexible support in many young dicot organs
rows.explanation: Living collenchyma supports growing organs without preventing bending.

rows.label: The characteristic wall thickening in angular collenchyma
rows.explanation: Corner thickening commonly contains cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin.

rows.label: The maturity condition of most sclerenchyma cells
rows.explanation: Most sclerenchyma loses its protoplast at maturity and provides mechanical strength.

rows.label: The elongated tapering cells of sclerenchyma
rows.explanation: Fibres are long supportive cells, often occurring in bundles.

rows.label: The sclerenchyma cells responsible for grittiness in pear flesh
rows.explanation: Stone cells or sclereids give pears a gritty texture.

rows.label: The simple tissue commonly containing conspicuous intercellular spaces
rows.explanation: Many parenchymatous tissues have spaces between neighbouring cells.

rows.label: The vascular tissue mainly transporting water and mineral ions
rows.explanation: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals from roots toward aerial parts.

rows.label: The living component of mature xylem
rows.explanation: Xylem parenchyma retains living protoplasts and contributes to storage and lateral transport.

rows.label: The elongated lignified conducting cells with tapering ends and no perforated end walls
rows.explanation: Water passes between tracheids through pits rather than open end perforations.

rows.label: The xylem elements joined through perforated end walls
rows.explanation: Vessel elements form continuous conducting tubes through their perforations.

rows.label: The openings in secondary walls that allow lateral movement between xylem cells
rows.explanation: Pits are regions with reduced secondary wall deposition and permit cell-to-cell transport.

rows.label: The first-formed primary xylem
rows.explanation: Protoxylem differentiates before metaxylem.

rows.label: The later-formed primary xylem
rows.explanation: Metaxylem develops after the earliest primary xylem elements.

rows.label: The protoxylem position in an exarch arrangement
rows.explanation: Exarch xylem has peripheral protoxylem and more central metaxylem.

rows.label: The protoxylem position in an endarch arrangement
rows.explanation: Endarch protoxylem lies nearer the centre and metaxylem nearer the periphery.

rows.label: The role mainly associated with xylem fibres
rows.explanation: Thick lignified fibres strengthen the xylem tissue.

rows.label: The vascular tissue chiefly transporting sugars from sources to sinks
rows.explanation: Phloem distributes products of photosynthesis and other organic solutes.

rows.label: The main conducting elements of angiosperm phloem
rows.explanation: Sieve-tube elements form the principal long-distance sugar-conducting pathway.

rows.label: The specialised end wall between adjacent sieve-tube elements
rows.explanation: Sieve plates contain pores connecting the cytoplasm of successive sieve-tube elements.

rows.label: The nuclear condition of a mature angiosperm sieve-tube element
wrong: Numerous chloroplast genomes replacing all cytoplasm
rows.explanation: Mature sieve-tube elements are living but enucleate and supported by companion cells.

rows.label: The living cells closely associated with angiosperm sieve tubes
rows.explanation: Companion cells help maintain sieve-tube metabolism and transport.

rows.label: The cytoplasmic connections between sieve tubes and companion cells
rows.explanation: Plasmodesmata connect these closely associated living cells.

rows.label: The phloem component commonly absent in most monocots
rows.explanation: The textbook notes that phloem parenchyma is absent in most monocotyledons.

rows.label: The phloem component that is generally dead at maturity
rows.explanation: Sclerenchymatous phloem fibres provide support.

rows.label: The earlier-formed primary phloem
rows.explanation: Protophloem develops before metaphloem.

rows.label: The later-formed primary phloem
rows.explanation: Metaphloem is the later primary phloem, not a form of xylem.

rows.label: The outermost cell layer of the primary plant body
rows.explanation: The epidermis forms the external protective covering of primary organs.

rows.label: The waxy protective layer commonly covering aerial epidermis
rows.explanation: Cutin-containing cuticle limits water loss from aerial surfaces.

rows.label: The epidermal extension responsible for most young-root absorption
rows.explanation: Root hairs are unicellular extensions increasing absorptive area.

rows.label: The number of guard cells usually surrounding a stomatal pore
rows.explanation: A pair of guard cells regulates the stomatal aperture.

rows.label: The typical guard-cell shape in grasses
rows.explanation: Grass guard cells characteristically have expanded ends and a narrow middle.

rows.label: The guard-cell shape common in many dicot leaves
rows.explanation: Many nongrass angiosperms possess kidney-shaped guard cells.

rows.label: The relative thickness of the guard-cell wall bordering the stomatal pore
wrong: Thinner than the outer wall in all cases
rows.explanation: Differential wall thickness helps convert turgor changes into pore movement.

rows.label: The epidermal cells adjoining guard cells and structurally distinct from ordinary epidermis
rows.explanation: Subsidiary cells form part of the stomatal complex.

rows.label: The combined unit of pore, guard cells and associated subsidiary cells
rows.explanation: The stomatal apparatus includes the pore and its surrounding specialised cells.

rows.label: The multicellular or unicellular hair-like outgrowths on many shoots
rows.explanation: Trichomes can reduce water loss and provide protection or secretion.

rows.label: The innermost cortical layer of a typical root
rows.explanation: Endodermis forms the boundary between cortex and vascular cylinder.

rows.label: The waterproofing substance associated with Casparian strips
rows.explanation: Suberin impregnation blocks unrestricted apoplastic movement across the endodermis.

rows.label: The layer immediately inside a typical root endodermis
rows.explanation: Pericycle surrounds the vascular tissues just within the endodermis.

rows.label: The tissue from which lateral roots commonly originate
rows.explanation: Lateral roots arise endogenously from pericycle cells.

rows.label: The arrangement with xylem and phloem on different alternating radii
rows.explanation: Radial bundles are characteristic of roots.

rows.label: The parenchyma between root xylem and phloem patches
rows.explanation: Conjunctive parenchyma lies between the separate conducting strands.

rows.label: The usual xylem maturation pattern of roots
rows.explanation: Root protoxylem is peripheral relative to metaxylem.

rows.label: The pith condition typical of a young dicot root
wrong: Entirely absent from every dicot root
rows.explanation: Typical dicot roots have little central pith compared with monocot roots.

rows.label: The pith condition typical of a monocot root
rows.explanation: A prominent central pith is a common monocot-root feature.

rows.label: The term describing numerous xylem poles in a monocot root
rows.explanation: Polyarch refers to many xylem strands, not the direction of xylem maturation.

rows.label: The usual arrangement of vascular bundles in a young dicot stem
rows.explanation: Dicot stem bundles typically form a ring surrounding the pith.

rows.label: The hypodermal tissue typical of a young dicot stem
rows.explanation: Collenchymatous hypodermis provides support beneath the epidermis.

rows.label: The common name for the starch-rich endodermis of a dicot stem
rows.explanation: Stem endodermal cells can accumulate conspicuous starch grains.

rows.label: The parenchymatous strips between vascular bundles in a dicot stem
rows.explanation: Medullary rays permit radial transport between central and peripheral tissues.

rows.label: The vascular bundle with cambium between xylem and phloem
rows.explanation: An open bundle retains cambium capable of producing secondary tissues.

rows.label: The vascular bundle lacking cambium
rows.explanation: Closed bundles lack a cambial strip between their conducting tissues.

rows.label: The hypodermal tissue typical of a monocot stem
rows.explanation: A sclerenchymatous hypodermis strengthens many monocot stems.

rows.label: The sheath surrounding individual vascular bundles in a typical monocot stem
rows.explanation: A supporting sclerenchymatous sheath encloses each bundle.

rows.label: The water-containing cavity associated with protoxylem breakdown in maize stem
rows.explanation: Stretching and disintegration of early xylem can create a protoxylem cavity.

rows.label: The tissue organisation outside bundles in a typical monocot stem
wrong: Distinct cortex and pith separated by a continuous cambium
rows.explanation: Monocot stems generally lack the sharply distinguished cortex and pith of dicot stems.
