rows.label: The tissue between the upper and lower epidermis of a leaf
rows.explanation: Leaf mesophyll is predominantly photosynthetic parenchyma.

rows.label: The tightly arranged elongated mesophyll cells in a dorsiventral leaf
rows.explanation: Palisade cells are densely packed and rich in chloroplasts.

rows.label: The loosely arranged mesophyll with extensive air spaces
rows.explanation: Air spaces in spongy mesophyll facilitate internal gas exchange.

rows.label: The surface commonly bearing more stomata in a dorsiventral dicot leaf
rows.explanation: Many dorsiventral leaves have more stomata on the lower epidermis.

rows.label: The leaf type with broadly similar upper and lower surfaces
rows.explanation: Many monocot leaves are isobilateral in internal organisation.

rows.label: The mesophyll differentiation common in isobilateral grass leaves
rows.explanation: Typical grass mesophyll is not separated into distinct palisade and spongy regions.

rows.label: The function of bulliform cells during water shortage
rows.correct: Promote leaf rolling after loss of turgor
rows.explanation: Loss of bulliform-cell turgor helps roll the leaf and reduce exposed surface.

rows.label: The usual position of xylem in a collateral leaf vein
rows.explanation: Xylem generally faces the adaxial side and phloem the abaxial side.

rows.label: The usual position of phloem in a collateral leaf vein
rows.explanation: Phloem is typically abaxial to the xylem in a leaf bundle.

rows.label: The cells enclosing a leaf vascular bundle
rows.explanation: A bundle sheath separates vascular tissue from surrounding mesophyll.

rows.label: The secondary tissue produced on the inner side of vascular cambium
rows.explanation: Vascular cambium adds secondary xylem inward and phloem outward.

rows.label: The secondary tissue produced on the outer side of vascular cambium
rows.explanation: New phloem is added external to the vascular cambium.

rows.label: The meristem also called phellogen
rows.explanation: Phellogen forms the protective periderm.

rows.label: The tissue produced outward by cork cambium
rows.explanation: Phellem or cork is produced toward the exterior.

rows.label: The tissue produced inward by cork cambium
rows.explanation: Phelloderm is the living secondary cortex produced inward.

rows.label: The collective unit of phellem, phellogen and phelloderm
rows.explanation: These three tissues together constitute the periderm.

rows.label: The loosely packed openings allowing gas exchange through bark
rows.explanation: Lenticels provide a pathway for gas diffusion through the periderm.

rows.label: The younger functional outer secondary xylem
rows.explanation: Sapwood participates actively in water conduction.

rows.label: The older central wood generally no longer conducting water
rows.explanation: Heartwood accumulates deposits and mainly provides support.

rows.label: The seasonal wood region usually having wider vessel lumina in temperate trees
rows.explanation: Favourable early-season growth commonly produces wider conducting elements than latewood.

rows.label: The organisational level formed by cells and intercellular material performing related functions
rows.explanation: A tissue combines cells and extracellular components for one or more related functions.

rows.label: The organisational level represented by the stomach
rows.explanation: The stomach contains several tissue types integrated into a functional structure.

rows.label: The organisational level represented by the digestive tract and associated glands together
rows.explanation: Cooperating organs make an organ system.

rows.label: The number of basic animal tissue types
rows.explanation: The basic types are epithelial, connective, muscular and neural tissue.

rows.label: The study of externally visible form and features
rows.explanation: Morphology describes outward form and structural appearance.

rows.label: The study of internal organs and their arrangement
rows.explanation: Anatomy examines internal structure and relationships among organs.

rows.label: The tissue forming continuous sheets over surfaces and linings
rows.explanation: Epithelia cover surfaces and line cavities, ducts and tubes.

rows.label: The tissue specialised for contraction
rows.explanation: Muscle cells generate force through interactions of contractile proteins.

rows.label: The tissue specialised for rapid electrical communication
rows.explanation: Neurons and supporting cells form neural tissue.

rows.label: The tissue category generally characterised by cells distributed in extracellular matrix
rows.explanation: Connective tissues vary widely in the composition of their matrix.

rows.label: The epithelial form with a single layer of thin flattened cells
rows.explanation: A thin simple squamous sheet allows rapid diffusion or filtration.

rows.label: The epithelial form with cube-like cells common in kidney tubules
rows.explanation: Cuboidal epithelium is suited to secretion and absorption in many tubules.

rows.label: The epithelial form with tall cells common in the intestinal lining
rows.explanation: Columnar absorptive cells commonly line the intestine.

rows.label: The epithelial specialisation moving material along a surface
rows.explanation: Coordinated ciliary beating moves mucus or other material across epithelia.

rows.label: The type of epithelial junction that limits leakage between cells
rows.explanation: Tight junctions seal intercellular spaces.

rows.label: The type of junction permitting direct exchange of small molecules between adjacent cells
rows.explanation: Gap junction channels allow small solutes and ions to pass between cells.

rows.label: The connective-tissue cells specialised for fat storage
rows.explanation: Adipocytes contain lipid reserves and also contribute to insulation and cushioning.

rows.label: The cells residing within cartilage lacunae
rows.explanation: Chondrocytes maintain the cartilage matrix.

rows.label: The cells residing in mature bone lacunae
rows.explanation: Osteocytes are mature bone cells embedded within mineralised matrix.

rows.label: The connective tissue joining one bone to another at a joint
rows.explanation: Ligaments stabilise joints; tendons usually connect muscle to bone.

rows.label: The class of the frog
rows.explanation: Frogs are amphibian vertebrates capable of life in water and on land.

rows.label: The phylum of the frog
rows.explanation: Frogs possess chordate features and a vertebral column.

rows.label: The temperature pattern described as poikilothermy in frogs
rows.correct: Body temperature varies with environmental temperature
wrong: The body produces no heat at all
rows.explanation: Frog body temperature changes substantially with environmental conditions.

rows.label: The summer dormancy of a frog during extreme heat
rows.explanation: Aestivation reduces activity during hot or dry conditions.

rows.label: The winter dormancy of a frog during severe cold
rows.explanation: Hibernation is a dormant state associated with winter conditions.

rows.label: The protective benefit of a frog blending with its surroundings
rows.explanation: Background matching reduces the chance of detection by predators.

rows.label: The secretion that makes frog skin slippery and moist
rows.explanation: Skin mucous glands help maintain a moist surface.

rows.label: The important route of water uptake in a frog
rows.explanation: Frogs absorb water across their permeable skin.

rows.label: The main external body regions of an adult frog
wrong: Head, neck, thorax and abdomen with a long tail
rows.explanation: Adult frogs have no distinct neck or tail.

rows.label: The membrane protecting a frog's eye in water
rows.explanation: The nictitating membrane covers and protects the eye.

rows.label: The visible membrane receiving sound vibrations in a frog
rows.explanation: The tympanum transmits sound vibrations to the middle ear.

rows.label: The number of digits on each frog forelimb
rows.explanation: The frog forelimb ends in four digits.

rows.label: The number of digits on each frog hindlimb
rows.explanation: The hindfoot has five digits, commonly connected by webbing.

rows.label: The principal benefit of webbed hindfoot digits
rows.explanation: Webbing increases the surface that pushes against water.

rows.label: The limbs chiefly providing propulsive force during a frog's leap
rows.explanation: Large muscular hindlimbs generate the main jumping force.

rows.label: The sound-amplifying structures characteristic of male frogs in the textbook
rows.explanation: Vocal sacs help amplify mating calls.

rows.label: The male frog structure assisting grip during amplexus
rows.correct: Copulatory pad on the first forelimb digit
rows.explanation: The nuptial or copulatory pad improves grip on the female.

rows.label: The usual adult frog diet
rows.explanation: Adult frogs capture animal prey and can help control insect populations.

rows.label: The organ used to capture prey in a frog
rows.explanation: The tongue is rapidly projected to catch prey.

rows.label: The short tube connecting the pharynx to the stomach in a frog
rows.explanation: The oesophagus carries swallowed food to the stomach.

rows.label: The acid secreted into the frog stomach
wrong: Acetic acid as the main gastric acid
rows.explanation: Hydrochloric acid creates an acidic environment for gastric digestion.

rows.label: The partly digested food passing from stomach to small intestine
rows.explanation: Chyme is the partially digested gastric mixture.

rows.label: The first region of the frog small intestine
rows.explanation: The duodenum receives the contents of the stomach and digestive secretions.

rows.label: The organ producing bile in a frog
rows.explanation: Bile is synthesised by the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

rows.label: The storage organ for bile in a frog
rows.explanation: The gall bladder stores bile before it enters the intestine.

rows.label: The main digestive action of bile
rows.explanation: Bile disperses fat into small droplets and is not a digestive enzyme.

rows.label: The gland producing pancreatic digestive juice in a frog
rows.explanation: The pancreas secretes enzymes that participate in intestinal digestion.

rows.label: The chamber through which frog intestinal wastes leave the body
rows.explanation: The rectum opens into the cloaca, a common terminal chamber.

rows.label: Gas exchange through a frog's skin
rows.explanation: A moist, vascular skin permits diffusion of respiratory gases.

rows.label: Gas exchange through the frog's lungs
rows.explanation: Pulmonary respiration occurs across the internal lung surface.

rows.label: The principal gas-exchange surface during frog hibernation
rows.explanation: Cutaneous gas exchange supports the dormant frog.

rows.label: The main mechanism of oxygen movement across frog skin
wrong: Bulk swallowing of oxygen bubbles only
rows.explanation: Oxygen moves down its partial-pressure gradient across the moist skin.

rows.label: The normal sequence of air entry toward a frog's lungs
rows.explanation: Air reaches the lungs through the nostrils and buccal cavity.

rows.label: The blood-vessel organisation of a frog
rows.explanation: Blood normally remains within the heart and a connected vessel network.

rows.label: The chamber composition of a frog heart
rows.explanation: A frog's three main cardiac chambers include two atria and a common ventricle.

rows.label: The membrane enclosing the frog heart
rows.explanation: The pericardium surrounds and protects the heart.

rows.label: The cardiac chamber receiving blood from the sinus venosus
rows.explanation: The sinus venosus drains into the right atrium.

rows.label: The outflow structure receiving blood from the frog ventricle
rows.explanation: The ventricle pumps blood into the conus arteriosus.

rows.label: The portal connection carrying blood from intestine toward liver
rows.explanation: The hepatic portal system takes absorbed substances to the liver.

rows.label: The portal connection carrying blood from posterior body regions toward kidneys
rows.explanation: Frogs have a renal portal circulation associated with the kidneys.

rows.label: The nuclear condition of mature frog erythrocytes
wrong: Containing two nuclei in every cell
rows.explanation: Frog red blood cells retain a nucleus, unlike mature mammalian erythrocytes.

rows.label: The respiratory pigment within frog erythrocytes
rows.explanation: Haemoglobin binds and transports oxygen in frog blood.

rows.label: The blood component normally absent from frog lymph
rows.explanation: Lymph normally lacks red blood cells but can contain white cells.

rows.label: The number of kidneys in a normal adult frog
rows.explanation: A pair of kidneys lies dorsally, one on each side of the vertebral column.

rows.label: The structural and functional unit of a frog kidney
rows.explanation: Nephrons filter and modify fluid to form urine.

rows.label: The principal nitrogenous waste of an adult frog
wrong: Ammonia as the sole adult waste
rows.explanation: Adult frogs are described as ureotelic because urea is their main nitrogenous waste.

rows.label: The ducts carrying urine away from frog kidneys
rows.explanation: Ureters carry urine to the cloaca.

rows.label: The dual role of the male frog ureter
rows.explanation: Male ureters function as urinogenital ducts.

rows.label: The relation of urinary and reproductive ducts in a female frog
rows.correct: Ureters and oviducts open separately into the cloaca
wrong: Both are one continuous duct from the ovary
rows.explanation: Female urinary and reproductive pathways remain separate until the cloaca.

rows.label: The position of the frog urinary bladder relative to the rectum
rows.explanation: The thin-walled urinary bladder lies ventral to the rectum.

rows.label: The organs forming the frog central nervous system
rows.explanation: The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord.

rows.label: The structures forming the frog peripheral nervous system
rows.explanation: Peripheral nerves connect the CNS with body tissues.

rows.label: The number of pairs of cranial nerves in a frog
rows.explanation: The textbook describes ten cranial nerve pairs in frogs.

rows.label: The bony enclosure protecting the frog brain
rows.explanation: The cranium forms the brain box.

rows.label: The brain region containing the frog's paired optic lobes
rows.explanation: The midbrain is prominently associated with paired optic lobes.

rows.label: The pair of major structures forming the frog hindbrain
rows.explanation: The cerebellum and medulla are hindbrain components.

rows.label: The brain region continuing into the spinal cord
rows.explanation: The medulla is continuous with the spinal cord through the foramen magnum.

rows.label: The opening through which the medulla continues out of the cranium
rows.explanation: The foramen magnum connects the cranial and spinal cavities.

rows.label: The sensory surface chiefly responsible for smell in a frog
rows.explanation: Olfactory receptors occur in the nasal lining.

rows.label: The additional sensory function of the frog inner ear besides hearing
rows.explanation: The inner ear participates in balance as well as hearing.

rows.label: The number of testes in a normal male frog
rows.explanation: Male frogs possess a pair of testes near the kidneys.

rows.label: The peritoneal fold attaching the testis near the kidney
rows.explanation: The mesorchium supports the testis.

rows.label: The small ducts carrying sperm from a frog testis toward the kidney
rows.explanation: Vasa efferentia connect the testis to the renal sperm-transport pathway.

rows.label: The kidney canal receiving frog vasa efferentia
wrong: Central canal of the spinal cord
rows.explanation: Bidder's canal receives sperm and communicates with the urinogenital duct.

rows.label: The functional connection between female frog ovaries and kidneys
wrong: Ova must pass through renal tubules
rows.explanation: Ovaries lie near kidneys but have a separate reproductive pathway.

rows.label: The site of fertilisation in the textbook frog life cycle
wrong: Inside a shelled egg before laying
rows.explanation: Frogs release gametes into water where fertilisation occurs.

rows.label: The larval stage of a frog
rows.explanation: Frog eggs hatch into aquatic tadpoles.

rows.label: The transformation from tadpole to adult frog
rows.explanation: Metamorphosis reorganises larval structures for adult life.

rows.label: The main thyroid hormone associated with tadpole metamorphosis
rows.explanation: Thyroid hormones control major developmental changes during amphibian metamorphosis.

rows.label: The ecological benefit of insect-eating frogs near crops
rows.correct: Reduction of some insect pest populations
wrong: Direct nitrogen fixation by frog skin
rows.explanation: Predation on insects can help limit crop pests and contributes to food-web balance.

rows.label: First observer of a live cell
rows.explanation: Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell.

rows.label: Scientist who discovered the nucleus
rows.explanation: Robert Brown discovered the nucleus; the chapter separately credits Leeuwenhoek with observing live cells.

rows.label: Botanist who studied plant tissues in 1838
rows.explanation: Schleiden concluded that plants consist of cells forming tissues.

rows.label: Scientist who studied animal cells in 1839
rows.explanation: Schwann reported a thin outer plasma membrane around animal cells.

rows.label: Scientist associated with Omnis cellula-e cellula
rows.explanation: Virchow explained that new cells arise through division of pre-existing cells.

rows.label: Basic structural and functional unit of life
rows.explanation: A cell can support the fundamental functions of life; subcellular components do not independently constitute living organisms.

rows.label: Principal arena of cellular activities
rows.explanation: The cytoplasm is the main arena for many chemical reactions that maintain the living state.

rows.label: Defining nuclear feature of prokaryotes
wrong: Presence of a nucleolus within an envelope
rows.explanation: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus, whereas eukaryotes possess one.

rows.label: Non-membranous organelle present in both cell types
rows.explanation: Ribosomes occur in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and are not surrounded by a membrane.

rows.label: Typical animal-cell structure largely absent from plant cells
rows.explanation: The chapter contrasts the animal centrosome with plant-specific walls, plastids and large vacuoles.

rows.label: Example of a prokaryotic organism
rows.explanation: Bacteria, cyanobacteria and mycoplasmas are listed as prokaryotes.

rows.label: Shape described by the term bacillus
rows.explanation: Bacillus denotes a rod-shaped bacterium.

rows.label: Shape described by the term coccus
rows.explanation: Cocci are spherical bacteria.

rows.label: Shape described by the term vibrio
rows.explanation: Vibrios have a comma-like shape.

rows.label: Shape described by the term spirillum
rows.explanation: Spirilla are spiral-shaped bacteria.

rows.label: Prokaryotic group lacking a cell wall
rows.explanation: Mycoplasmas are the exception to the usual prokaryotic cell wall.

rows.label: Small extra-chromosomal circular bacterial DNA
rows.explanation: Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules separate from bacterial genomic DNA; they may confer antibiotic resistance.

rows.label: Outer-to-inner order of a typical bacterial envelope
rows.explanation: The three envelope layers act together but have distinct structures.

rows.label: Loose bacterial glycocalyx
rows.explanation: A loose glycocalyx is a slime layer; a thick and tough one is a capsule.

rows.label: Thick and tough bacterial glycocalyx
rows.explanation: Capsules and slime layers are alternative forms of glycocalyx.

rows.label: Bacterial component that determines shape and resists bursting
rows.explanation: The wall supplies structural support and protects against bursting or collapse.

rows.label: Pigment-bearing membranous extensions in cyanobacteria
rows.explanation: Chromatophores contain pigments in photosynthetic prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria.

rows.label: Longest portion of a bacterial flagellum
rows.explanation: A bacterial flagellum consists of a filament, hook and basal body; the filament extends from the cell surface.

rows.label: Role of bacterial fimbriae described in the chapter
rows.explanation: Fimbriae help attachment to surfaces; they are distinguished from motile flagella.

rows.label: Sedimentation coefficient of prokaryotic ribosomes
rows.explanation: A prokaryotic ribosome is 70S and contains 50S and 30S subunits.

rows.label: Large subunit of a prokaryotic ribosome
rows.explanation: The two prokaryotic subunits are 50S and 30S; sedimentation values are not arithmetically additive.

rows.label: Multiple ribosomes translating one mRNA
rows.explanation: A polysome consists of several ribosomes associated with a single messenger RNA.

rows.label: Membrane status of prokaryotic reserve inclusion bodies
rows.explanation: Phosphate granules and glycogen granules are examples of non-membranous reserve inclusions.

rows.label: Special inclusions in photosynthetic bacteria
rows.explanation: Gas vacuoles occur in blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria.

rows.label: Plant-cell structure responsible for a rigid external boundary
rows.explanation: Plant cells have a wall external to the plasma membrane; animal cells do not.

rows.label: Orientation of phospholipid polar heads in a bilayer
rows.explanation: Polar heads face the aqueous surroundings, shielding nonpolar tails inside the membrane.

rows.label: Orientation of phospholipid hydrocarbon tails
rows.explanation: The nonpolar tails face inward and are protected from the aqueous environment.

rows.label: Approximate protein proportion in human erythrocyte membrane
rows.explanation: The chapter gives about 52% protein and 40% lipid for the human erythrocyte membrane.

rows.label: Approximate lipid proportion in human erythrocyte membrane
rows.explanation: Membrane composition varies among cells; the erythrocyte example contains about 40% lipid.

rows.label: Membrane proteins lying on its surface
rows.explanation: Peripheral proteins lie on the membrane surface, while integral proteins are partly or fully buried.

rows.label: Scientists who proposed the fluid mosaic model
rows.explanation: Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model in 1972.

rows.label: Membrane property permitting lateral protein movement
wrong: Permanent covalent bonds between all lipids
rows.explanation: Lipid fluidity permits lateral movement of proteins within the bilayer.

rows.label: Movement of water by diffusion across a membrane
rows.explanation: Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane.

rows.label: Transport against a concentration gradient
rows.explanation: Movement from lower to higher concentration requires energy, for example ATP-driven sodium/potassium pumping.

rows.label: Main cementing material of middle lamella
rows.explanation: The middle lamella is mainly calcium pectate and holds neighbouring cells together.

rows.label: Channels connecting neighbouring plant-cell cytoplasm
rows.explanation: Plasmodesmata traverse cell walls and connect adjacent cytoplasms.

rows.label: Position of secondary wall relative to primary wall
rows.explanation: The secondary wall is laid down toward the plasma membrane, internal to the primary wall.

rows.label: Organelle included in the endomembrane system
rows.explanation: The coordinated endomembrane system includes ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles.

rows.label: Organelle excluded from the endomembrane system
rows.explanation: Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are excluded because their functions are not coordinated with that system.

rows.label: Feature distinguishing rough ER from smooth ER
rows.explanation: Ribosomes attached to the surface make ER appear rough.

rows.label: Cell activity associated with abundant rough ER
rows.explanation: Rough ER is abundant in cells engaged in protein synthesis and secretion.

rows.label: Major biosynthetic role of smooth ER
rows.explanation: Smooth ER is a major site of lipid synthesis and produces steroid hormones in animal cells.

rows.label: Discoverer of Golgi apparatus in 1898
rows.explanation: Camillo Golgi first observed the densely stained reticular structures near the nucleus.

rows.label: Receiving face of Golgi apparatus
rows.explanation: The cis or forming face receives ER-derived material; the trans face is the maturing face.

rows.label: Maturing face of Golgi apparatus
rows.explanation: Material travels through the Golgi toward its trans or maturing face.

rows.label: Compounds formed by Golgi processing
rows.explanation: Golgi processing includes modification and packaging, including formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids.

rows.label: Characteristic lysosomal enzymes
rows.explanation: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that work optimally at acidic pH.

rows.label: Membrane around a vacuole
rows.explanation: The tonoplast is the single membrane enclosing the vacuole.

rows.label: Function of the contractile vacuole in Amoeba
rows.explanation: The contractile vacuole removes excess water and participates in excretion.

rows.label: Approximate maximum vacuolar share of plant-cell volume in the chapter
rows.explanation: In some plant cells the vacuole occupies up to 90% of cell volume.

rows.label: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane
rows.explanation: Cristae increase the inner mitochondrial membrane surface area.

rows.label: Inner compartment of a mitochondrion
rows.explanation: The mitochondrial matrix is enclosed by the inner membrane.

rows.label: Major energy product associated with mitochondria
rows.explanation: Mitochondria are sites of aerobic respiration and ATP production.

rows.label: Ribosomes in the mitochondrial matrix
rows.explanation: The matrix contains small 70S ribosomes as well as circular DNA and RNA.

rows.label: Mode of mitochondrial multiplication stated in the chapter
rows.explanation: Mitochondria divide by fission.

rows.label: Plastids rich in yellow orange or red carotenoids
rows.explanation: Chromoplast pigments include carotene and xanthophylls.

rows.label: Leucoplasts storing starch
rows.explanation: Amyloplasts store carbohydrates such as starch.

rows.label: Leucoplasts storing oils and fats
rows.explanation: Elaioplasts store lipids.

rows.label: Leucoplasts storing proteins
rows.explanation: Aleuroplasts are the protein-storing leucoplasts.

rows.label: Stacks of thylakoids
rows.explanation: Thylakoids are arranged into stacks called grana.

rows.label: Membranes connecting grana
rows.explanation: Stroma lamellae connect the thylakoids of different grana.

rows.label: Location of chlorophyll within a chloroplast
rows.explanation: Chlorophyll pigments are located in thylakoid membranes.

rows.label: Fluid compartment of chloroplast containing synthetic enzymes
rows.explanation: The stroma contains enzymes for carbohydrate and protein synthesis, DNA and ribosomes.

rows.label: Scientist who first observed ribosomes in 1953
rows.explanation: Palade observed ribosomes as dense particles under the electron microscope.

rows.label: Large subunit of a cytoplasmic eukaryotic ribosome
rows.explanation: An 80S eukaryotic ribosome has 60S and 40S subunits.

rows.label: Meaning of S in ribosomal sedimentation values
rows.explanation: S is the sedimentation coefficient expressed in Svedberg units and reflects size and density.

rows.label: Non-membranous network providing shape and mechanical support
rows.explanation: Microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments provide support, motility and shape.

rows.label: Core of a eukaryotic cilium or flagellum
rows.explanation: The membrane-covered axoneme is the microtubular core of cilia and flagella.

rows.label: Typical axonemal microtubule arrangement
rows.correct: Nine peripheral doublets and two central singlets
wrong: Nine peripheral triplets and no central pair
Eight peripheral doublets and one central pair
rows.explanation: The 9+2 arrangement includes nine doublets surrounding two central microtubules.

rows.label: Links between peripheral axonemal doublets and central sheath
rows.explanation: Radial spokes connect peripheral doublets to the central sheath.

rows.label: Structures from which cilia and flagella emerge
rows.explanation: Cilia and flagella arise from centriole-like basal bodies.

rows.label: Relative orientation of centrioles in a centrosome
rows.explanation: A centrosome usually contains two centrioles lying perpendicular to each other.

rows.label: Peripheral microtubule arrangement of a centriole
rows.explanation: A centriole has nine evenly spaced peripheral microtubule triplets.

rows.label: Protein forming centriolar microtubules
rows.explanation: The peripheral fibrils of centrioles are made of tubulin.

rows.label: Nuclear-envelope membrane continuous with ER
wrong: Both membranes directly continuous with cristae
rows.explanation: The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with ER and bears ribosomes.

rows.label: Structures allowing RNA and protein movement across nuclear envelope
rows.explanation: Pores form where the two nuclear membranes fuse and provide passage between nucleus and cytoplasm.

rows.label: Mammalian cells cited as lacking nuclei
rows.explanation: The chapter identifies mammalian erythrocytes and plant sieve-tube cells as examples lacking nuclei.

rows.label: Major biosynthetic role of nucleolus
rows.explanation: The nucleolus is a non-membranous region involved in active ribosomal RNA synthesis.

rows.label: Basic proteins associated with chromatin
rows.explanation: Chromatin contains DNA, histones, non-histone proteins and RNA.

rows.label: Primary constriction of a chromosome
rows.explanation: The centromere holds sister chromatids together and bears kinetochores.

rows.label: Chromosome with a median centromere and equal arms
rows.explanation: A metacentric chromosome has its centromere in the middle and two equal arms.

rows.label: Chromosome with a slightly off-centre centromere
rows.explanation: A submetacentric chromosome has a slightly displaced centromere and unequal arms.

rows.label: Chromosome with a centromere near one end and very unequal arms
rows.explanation: An acrocentric chromosome has one very short arm and one very long arm.

rows.label: Chromosome with a terminal centromere
rows.explanation: In a telocentric chromosome the centromere lies at the terminal end.

rows.label: Small chromosome segment beyond a secondary constriction
rows.explanation: A secondary constriction can give a small chromosome fragment the appearance of a satellite.

rows.label: Acid used to grind tissue for chemical analysis
rows.explanation: The supplied protocol grinds living tissue in trichloroacetic acid before filtration.

rows.label: Filtrate obtained after straining the tissue slurry
rows.explanation: Small soluble compounds pass into the filtrate, called the acid-soluble pool.

rows.label: Material retained after straining the tissue slurry
rows.explanation: The retentate is the acid-insoluble fraction.

rows.label: Tissue mass remaining after water is evaporated
rows.explanation: Drying removes water; the residue supplies the tissue's dry weight.

rows.label: Residue left after complete burning of dried tissue
rows.explanation: Organic compounds are oxidised and lost as gases; ash contains inorganic elements.

rows.label: Element more abundant in living tissue than crust in Table 9.1
rows.explanation: Carbon is 18.5% of human body weight versus 0.03% of the crust in the table.

rows.label: Most abundant element by weight in the human-body column
rows.explanation: Table 9.1 lists oxygen at 65.0%, greater than carbon, hydrogen or nitrogen.

rows.label: Element abundant in crust but negligible in human-body column
rows.explanation: Silicon is 27.7% in the crust column but negligible in the human-body column.

rows.label: Carbon bearing both amino and carboxyl groups in protein amino acids
rows.explanation: Protein amino acids have amino and carboxyl groups attached to the same alpha carbon.

rows.label: Group primarily distinguishing one protein amino acid from another
rows.explanation: Variation in the R group distinguishes the amino acids.

rows.label: Number of common amino-acid types in proteins given here
rows.explanation: The chapter identifies twenty types of proteinaceous amino acids.

rows.label: R group of glycine
rows.explanation: Glycine has hydrogen as its R group.

rows.label: R group of alanine
rows.explanation: Alanine has a methyl side chain.

rows.label: R group of serine
rows.explanation: Serine has a hydroxymethyl R group.

rows.label: Acidic amino acid listed in the chapter
rows.explanation: Glutamic acid is classified as acidic according to its amino and carboxyl groups.

rows.label: Basic amino acid listed in the chapter
rows.explanation: Lysine is the example of a basic amino acid.

rows.label: Neutral amino acid explicitly used as an example
rows.explanation: The chapter lists valine as neutral, lysine as basic and glutamic acid as acidic.

rows.label: Aromatic amino acid among these choices
rows.explanation: Tyrosine, phenylalanine and tryptophan are the aromatic amino acids named here.

rows.label: Main reason amino-acid ionic form changes with pH
rows.explanation: The amino and carboxyl groups gain or lose protons as pH changes.

rows.label: Typical solubility property of lipids
rows.explanation: Lipids are generally insoluble in water.

rows.label: Total carbon atoms in palmitic acid
rows.explanation: Palmitic acid contains sixteen carbons, including the carboxyl carbon.

rows.label: Total carbon atoms in arachidonic acid
rows.explanation: Arachidonic acid contains twenty carbons, including the carboxyl carbon.

rows.label: Feature defining an unsaturated fatty acid
rows.correct: At least one carbon-carbon double bond
wrong: A nitrogenous base joined to sugar
rows.explanation: Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more C=C bonds; saturated fatty acids lack them.

rows.label: Chemical description of glycerol
rows.explanation: Glycerol is a three-carbon alcohol bearing three hydroxyl groups.

rows.label: Bonding of fatty acids to glycerol in glycerides
rows.explanation: Fatty acids are esterified to glycerol in mono-, di- and triglycerides.

rows.label: Property explaining why oils remain liquid in winter
rows.explanation: The chapter distinguishes oils from fats by their lower melting points.

rows.label: Membrane phospholipid example
rows.explanation: Lecithin is a phospholipid containing phosphorus and is associated with cell membranes.

rows.label: Base joined to sugar without phosphate
rows.explanation: A nucleoside contains a nitrogenous base and sugar but no phosphate group.

rows.label: Base sugar and phosphate together
rows.explanation: Adding phosphate to the sugar of a nucleoside gives a nucleotide.

rows.label: Example of a nucleoside
rows.explanation: Adenosine is a nucleoside; adenylic acid is its nucleotide form.

rows.label: Example of a nucleotide
rows.explanation: Adenylic acid includes base, sugar and phosphate.

rows.label: Metabolites with recognised normal physiological roles
rows.explanation: Primary metabolites include amino acids and sugars with identifiable physiological functions.

rows.label: Secondary-metabolite category containing morphine and codeine
rows.explanation: Table 9.3 lists morphine and codeine under alkaloids.

rows.label: Secondary-metabolite category containing abrin and ricin
rows.explanation: Abrin and ricin are listed as toxins.

rows.label: Secondary-metabolite category containing Concanavalin A
rows.explanation: Concanavalin A appears in the lectin category.

rows.label: Secondary-metabolite category containing carotenoids
rows.explanation: Carotenoids and anthocyanins are pigment examples.

rows.label: Approximate molecular-mass range of acid-soluble compounds
rows.explanation: The acid-soluble pool contains molecules of roughly 18–800 daltons.

rows.label: Small molecules that nevertheless enter the acid-insoluble fraction
rows.explanation: Membrane lipids form insoluble vesicular fragments after grinding, despite their small molecular masses.

rows.label: Reason membrane lipids enter the insoluble pellet
wrong: Every lipid is a giant polymer
They turn into protein during grinding
rows.explanation: Disrupted membranes form insoluble vesicles that separate with the macromolecular fraction.

rows.label: Most abundant chemical in living cells
rows.explanation: Water is the most abundant component; Table 9.4 gives a range of 70–90%.

rows.label: Protein proportion of total cellular mass in Table 9.4
rows.explanation: The table gives proteins as 10–15% of total cellular mass.

rows.label: Monomers of polypeptides
rows.explanation: Proteins are linear polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds.

rows.label: Bonds connecting amino acids in a protein backbone
rows.explanation: Amino acids in polypeptide chains are linked by peptide bonds.

rows.label: Polymer category applicable to proteins
rows.explanation: Proteins use different amino-acid monomers and are heteropolymers.

rows.label: Amino acids that must be supplied in the diet
rows.explanation: Essential amino acids must be obtained from food; non-essential ones can be synthesised by the body.

rows.label: Protein functioning as a hormone in Table 9.5
rows.explanation: Insulin is listed as a hormone.

rows.label: Protein enabling glucose entry into cells in Table 9.5
rows.explanation: GLUT-4 is identified as a glucose transporter.

rows.label: Protein defending against infectious agents
rows.explanation: Antibodies help fight infectious agents.

rows.label: Most abundant protein in the animal world
rows.explanation: The chapter distinguishes animal collagen from RuBisCO, the most abundant protein in the biosphere.

rows.label: Most abundant protein in the biosphere
rows.explanation: Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase is the biosphere's most abundant protein.

rows.label: Monomer of cellulose
rows.explanation: Cellulose is a glucose homopolymer.

rows.label: Storage polysaccharide in plants
rows.explanation: Starch serves as a store of energy in plant tissues.

rows.label: Storage polysaccharide described for animals
rows.explanation: Animals store carbohydrate as glycogen.

rows.label: Monomer of inulin
rows.explanation: Inulin is a polymer of fructose.

rows.label: Structural feature allowing starch to hold iodine
rows.explanation: Iodine fits within the helical portions of starch, giving a blue complex.

rows.label: Polysaccharide forming arthropod exoskeletons
rows.explanation: The chapter identifies chitin as the complex polysaccharide in arthropod exoskeletons.

rows.label: Building blocks of nucleic acids
rows.explanation: DNA and RNA are polynucleotides.

rows.label: Purine pair in nucleic acids
rows.explanation: Adenine and guanine are purines; cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines.

rows.label: Sugar characteristic of DNA
rows.explanation: DNA contains deoxyribose; RNA contains ribose.

rows.label: Sugar characteristic of RNA
rows.explanation: Ribose is the pentose sugar of RNA.

rows.label: Protein structural level specifying amino-acid sequence
rows.explanation: Primary structure records the order and positions of amino acids.

rows.label: First amino acid of a conventionally written polypeptide
rows.explanation: The first residue is N-terminal; the last is C-terminal.

rows.label: Protein structural level including alpha helices and beta sheets
rows.explanation: Local folding gives secondary structures such as helices and pleated sheets.

rows.label: Overall three-dimensional fold of one polypeptide
rows.explanation: Folding of a polypeptide upon itself gives its tertiary structure, important for biological activity.

rows.label: Arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits
rows.explanation: Quaternary structure describes how individual folded subunits are arranged relative to each other.

rows.label: Subunit composition of adult human haemoglobin
rows.correct: Two alpha and two beta chains
wrong: Two alpha and one beta chain
One alpha and one beta chain
rows.explanation: The four subunits of adult haemoglobin comprise two alpha and two beta chains.

rows.label: Catalytic nucleic acids
rows.explanation: Most enzymes are proteins, but catalytic nucleic acids are called ribozymes.

rows.label: Enzyme pocket into which substrate fits
rows.explanation: The active site is a crevice or pocket involved in substrate binding and catalysis.

rows.label: Enzymes retaining activity at 80–90°C in the chapter
rows.explanation: Enzymes from hot-environment organisms can be thermally stable at temperatures that damage many other enzymes.

rows.label: Quantity expressing reaction rate
rows.explanation: Reaction rate measures change in product amount per unit time.

rows.label: Enzyme accelerating carbon dioxide hydration
rows.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase accelerates formation of carbonic acid from carbon dioxide and water.

rows.label: Name for a sequence of enzyme-catalysed reactions
rows.explanation: A metabolic pathway consists of multiple reaction steps catalysed by enzymes or enzyme complexes.

rows.label: Anaerobic end product in skeletal muscle described here
rows.explanation: Under anaerobic conditions, skeletal muscle forms lactic acid.

rows.label: Fermentation product in yeast described here
rows.explanation: The chapter contrasts ethanol production in yeast with lactic acid formation in muscle.

rows.label: Obligatory transient complex before enzymatic conversion
rows.explanation: Substrate binding forms a short-lived ES complex before product release.

rows.label: Energy difference between substrate and transition state
rows.explanation: Activation energy is the barrier between the substrate state and transition state.

rows.label: Effect of an enzyme on the reaction energy barrier
rows.explanation: Enzymes lower the activation barrier and facilitate conversion without being consumed.

rows.label: Enzyme condition after product release
rows.correct: Available unchanged for another catalytic cycle
rows.explanation: The enzyme is released unchanged and can bind another substrate molecule.

rows.label: Cause of the plateau at high substrate concentration
rows.explanation: At saturation, no free enzyme molecules remain to bind additional substrate, so velocity reaches Vmax.

rows.label: Temperature at which a given enzyme shows maximum activity
rows.explanation: Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; activity falls away from those optima.

rows.label: Competitive inhibitor of succinic dehydrogenase cited here
rows.explanation: Malonate resembles succinate and competes for the substrate-binding site.

rows.label: Enzymes catalysing oxidation-reduction reactions
rows.explanation: Oxidoreductases mediate oxidation-reduction between substrates.

rows.label: Enzymes moving a non-hydrogen group between substrates
rows.explanation: Transferases transfer groups other than hydrogen from one substrate to another.

rows.label: Enzymes catalysing hydrolytic bond cleavage
rows.explanation: Hydrolases break specified bonds by hydrolysis.

rows.label: Enzymes removing groups without hydrolysis and leaving double bonds
rows.explanation: Lyases remove groups by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds.

rows.label: Enzymes interconverting optical geometric or positional isomers
rows.explanation: Isomerases catalyse interconversion between isomeric forms.

rows.label: Enzymes joining two compounds
rows.explanation: Ligases catalyse joining reactions, including formation of C–O, C–S, C–N or P–O bonds.

rows.label: Protein portion of an enzyme requiring a cofactor
rows.explanation: The apoenzyme is the protein component; its cofactor is a non-protein constituent.

rows.label: Tightly bound organic cofactor of peroxidase and catalase
rows.explanation: Haem is the prosthetic group associated with peroxidase and catalase.

rows.label: Metal cofactor of carboxypeptidase
rows.explanation: The chapter identifies zinc as the metal cofactor for carboxypeptidase.

rows.label: Sequence of genome duplication growth and division
rows.explanation: The cell cycle coordinates genome duplication, synthesis of cell constituents and division.

rows.label: Pattern of cytoplasmic growth across the cycle
rows.explanation: The chapter distinguishes continuous cell growth from DNA synthesis in one specific stage.

rows.label: Typical cycle length for cultured human cells in this example
rows.explanation: The chapter uses roughly 24 hours as an example, while noting variation among organisms and cell types.

rows.label: Example cycle length given for yeast
rows.explanation: Yeast may complete its cell cycle in about 90 minutes.

rows.label: Approximate time for division proper in the 24-hour example
rows.explanation: Actual division occupies about one hour, while interphase occupies most of the cycle.

rows.label: Fraction of the cycle occupied by interphase in the example
rows.explanation: Interphase lasts more than 95% of the described cycle.

rows.label: Phase between successive M phases
rows.explanation: Interphase lies between two successive M phases and includes growth and DNA replication.

rows.label: Division of the nucleus
rows.explanation: Karyokinesis separates duplicated genetic material into daughter nuclei.

rows.label: Division of the cytoplasm
rows.explanation: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and usually completes M phase.

rows.label: Correct order of interphase subdivisions
rows.explanation: G1 precedes DNA synthesis in S, which is followed by G2.

rows.label: Interval between mitosis and initiation of DNA replication
rows.explanation: G1 cells grow and remain metabolically active without replicating DNA.

rows.label: Phase of DNA replication
rows.explanation: The synthesis phase doubles DNA content.

rows.label: DNA amount after S if the G1 amount is 2C
rows.explanation: Replication doubles DNA from 2C to 4C.

rows.label: Chromosome number after S in an initially 2n cell
rows.explanation: DNA doubles in S phase but chromosome number, counted by centromeres, remains 2n.

rows.label: Phase of centriole duplication in animal cells
rows.explanation: Centriole duplication in the cytoplasm accompanies nuclear DNA replication during S phase.

rows.label: Phase of protein synthesis preparing directly for mitosis
rows.explanation: G2 includes growth and synthesis of proteins needed for mitosis.

rows.label: Phase from which non-dividing cells enter G0
rows.explanation: Cells exit G1 to enter the quiescent G0 state.

rows.label: Metabolic condition of cells in G0
rows.explanation: G0 cells remain metabolically active but do not proliferate unless called on to do so.

rows.label: Animal example of haploid cells dividing mitotically
rows.explanation: Male honey bees illustrate that mitosis need not be restricted to diploid cells.

rows.label: Plant cells capable of undergoing mitosis
rows.explanation: The chapter explicitly permits mitosis in both haploid and diploid plant cells.

rows.label: Chromosomes in an onion root-tip cell at G1 in the given example
rows.explanation: The supplied example states 16 chromosomes per onion root-tip cell.

rows.label: Chromosomes in the same onion cell immediately after S phase
rows.explanation: S phase doubles DNA, not chromosome number, so an initial 16 remains 16.

rows.label: Chromosomes in each daughter after mitosis of that onion cell
rows.explanation: Equational mitosis preserves the parent's chromosome number in each daughter.

rows.label: DNA content at G2 if each post-mitotic daughter has 2C
rows.explanation: S phase doubles DNA to 4C, which persists through G2 until division.

rows.label: Reason mitosis is called equational division
rows.correct: Parent and daughter chromosome numbers are equal
rows.explanation: Mitosis preserves chromosome number in the daughter nuclei.

rows.label: Number of conventional mitotic karyokinesis stages
rows.explanation: The four stages are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.

rows.label: First stage of mitotic karyokinesis
rows.explanation: Prophase follows interphase and begins chromosome condensation.

rows.label: Chromatin change initiating prophase
rows.explanation: Chromatin condenses and untangles to form compact mitotic chromosomes.

rows.label: Composition of each chromosome at completed prophase
rows.correct: Two chromatids joined at a centromere
wrong: Four homologues joined by a nucleolus
rows.explanation: Each replicated chromosome consists of two sister chromatids linked at its centromere.

rows.label: Movement of centrosomes during prophase
rows.explanation: Previously duplicated centrosomes begin moving toward opposite poles.

rows.label: Radiating microtubules around each animal centrosome
rows.explanation: The radial microtubules are asters; together with spindle fibres they form the mitotic apparatus.

rows.label: Structure no longer visible at the end of prophase in the account
rows.explanation: The nucleolus, nuclear envelope, Golgi and ER are not visible at the end of prophase.

rows.label: Event marking the start of metaphase in this chapter
rows.explanation: The supplied account places complete nuclear-envelope breakdown at the beginning of metaphase.

rows.label: Best mitotic stage for studying chromosome morphology
rows.explanation: Chromosomes are fully condensed and clearly visible at metaphase.

rows.label: Spindle-fibre attachment sites on chromosomes
rows.explanation: Kinetochores are disc-shaped structures at centromeres that attach spindle fibres.

rows.label: Position of chromosomes at mitotic metaphase
rows.explanation: Chromosomes align at the equator to form the metaphase plate.

rows.label: Spindle attachment of sister chromatids at metaphase
rows.explanation: Each sister kinetochore attaches to spindle fibres from a different pole.

rows.label: Event initiating mitotic anaphase
rows.explanation: Centromeres split and sister chromatids separate at anaphase onset.

rows.label: Leading portion of a chromosome during anaphase movement
rows.explanation: The centromere faces the pole and leads, while chromosome arms trail.

rows.label: Name for chromatids after separation in mitotic anaphase
rows.explanation: Once separated, each chromatid is a daughter chromosome destined for a daughter nucleus.

rows.label: Final stage of mitotic karyokinesis
rows.explanation: Telophase begins after chromosomes reach the poles.

rows.label: Chromosome change during telophase
rows.correct: Decondensation and loss of distinct individuality
rows.explanation: Chromosomes decondense into chromatin at the poles.

rows.label: Nuclear-envelope behaviour in telophase
rows.explanation: Two nuclear envelopes develop around the daughter chromosome sets.

rows.label: Organelle that reforms alongside nucleolus in telophase
rows.explanation: Golgi and ER reform during telophase, together with the nucleolus.

rows.label: Mechanism of animal-cell cytokinesis
rows.explanation: An inward-deepening furrow divides the animal cytoplasm.

rows.label: Mechanism of plant-cell cytokinesis
rows.correct: Cell plate formation from centre outward
wrong: Loss of the entire cell wall
rows.explanation: Plant cytokinesis begins centrally with a cell plate growing toward the lateral walls.

rows.label: Future intercellular layer represented by the cell plate
rows.explanation: The cell plate represents the future middle lamella between adjacent daughter-cell walls.

rows.label: Outcome of karyokinesis without cytokinesis
wrong: Immediate production of four isolated cells
rows.explanation: Nuclear division without cytoplasmic division can produce a syncytial multinucleate condition.

rows.label: Example of syncytial condition named in the chapter
rows.explanation: The chapter cites liquid coconut endosperm as an example of nuclei sharing undivided cytoplasm.

rows.label: Ratio restored by division after cell growth
rows.explanation: Growth disturbs the relation between nuclear and cytoplasmic contents; division helps restore it.

rows.label: Process primarily supporting replacement of damaged somatic cells
rows.explanation: Mitosis contributes to repair and replacement of epidermal, gut-lining and blood cells.

rows.label: Plant tissues whose mitosis supports continued growth
rows.explanation: Meristematic tissues divide repeatedly, supporting growth throughout plant life.

rows.label: Division reducing chromosome number by half
rows.explanation: Meiosis produces haploid products from a diploid parent cell.

rows.label: Process restoring diploidy after the haploid phase
rows.explanation: Fusion of haploid gametes restores the diploid chromosome complement.

rows.label: Number of DNA replication cycles before the two meiotic divisions
rows.explanation: Meiosis has two sequential divisions but only one preceding cycle of DNA replication.

rows.label: Number of successive nuclear divisions in meiosis
rows.explanation: Meiosis I and meiosis II follow a single replication cycle.

rows.label: Chromatids participating in meiotic crossing over
wrong: Only sister chromatids of one chromosome
rows.explanation: Recombination occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.

rows.label: Usual cellular products after completed meiosis II
rows.explanation: The chapter describes four haploid daughter cells at the end of meiosis II.

rows.label: Meiotic phase with five named substages
rows.explanation: Prophase I comprises leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis.

rows.label: First substage of prophase I
rows.explanation: Chromosomes become gradually visible and begin compaction during leptotene.

rows.label: Stage at which homologous chromosomes start pairing
rows.explanation: Synapsis begins in zygotene.

rows.label: Term for pairing of homologous chromosomes
rows.explanation: The association of homologous chromosomes during zygotene is called synapsis.

rows.label: Structure accompanying chromosome synapsis
rows.explanation: Electron microscopy reveals a synaptonemal complex associated with paired homologues.

rows.label: Pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes
rows.explanation: A bivalent contains two replicated homologous chromosomes and four chromatids.

rows.label: Number of chromatids in a tetrad
rows.explanation: Each of the two homologous chromosomes contributes two chromatids.

rows.label: Substage in which tetrads become clearly distinct
rows.explanation: The four chromatids of each bivalent become distinctly visible during pachytene.

rows.label: Substage characterised by recombination nodules
rows.explanation: Recombination nodules mark crossing-over sites during pachytene.

rows.label: Enzyme associated with crossing over in this chapter
rows.explanation: Crossing over is enzyme-mediated, involving recombinase.

rows.label: Consequence of crossing over
wrong: Immediate formation of a cell plate
rows.explanation: Exchange between homologous chromatids generates recombined genetic material.

rows.label: Substage by whose end recombination is completed
rows.explanation: The chapter places completion of recombination by the end of pachytene.

rows.label: Substage beginning with dissolution of synaptonemal complex
rows.explanation: In diplotene, homologues start separating as the synaptonemal complex dissolves.

rows.label: X-shaped connections visible between separating homologues
rows.explanation: Chiasmata mark crossover sites where homologues remain connected during diplotene.

rows.label: Prophase-I stage prolonged in some vertebrate oocytes
rows.explanation: Diplotene can last for months or years in oocytes of some vertebrates.

rows.label: Last substage of prophase I
rows.explanation: Diakinesis is the final prophase-I substage and leads into metaphase I.

rows.label: Characteristic chiasma event in diakinesis
rows.explanation: Terminalisation of chiasmata accompanies full chromosome condensation and spindle assembly.

rows.label: Units aligned at the equator in metaphase I
rows.explanation: Paired homologous chromosomes align as bivalents on the equatorial plate.

rows.label: Structures separating during anaphase I
rows.explanation: Homologues separate in anaphase I while sister chromatids remain associated.

rows.label: Centromere condition during anaphase I
rows.explanation: Anaphase I separates homologues without splitting the sister-centromere association.

rows.label: Cellular grouping after meiosis I and cytokinesis
rows.explanation: Telophase I followed by cytokinesis gives a dyad of cells.

rows.label: Interval between meiosis I and meiosis II
wrong: G1 of an ordinary full cycle
rows.explanation: Interkinesis is the usually short interval between the meiotic divisions.

rows.label: DNA replication during interkinesis
rows.explanation: The chapter explicitly states that DNA does not replicate during interkinesis.

rows.label: Division resembling ordinary mitosis
rows.explanation: Meiosis II resembles mitosis because sister chromatids are separated.

rows.label: Nuclear-envelope state by the end of prophase II
rows.explanation: The nuclear membrane disappears by the end of prophase II and chromosomes compact again.

rows.label: Chromosomal structures attached to opposite poles at metaphase II
rows.explanation: Opposite spindle poles attach to the kinetochores of sister chromatids at metaphase II.

rows.label: Event initiating anaphase II
rows.explanation: Centromere splitting releases sister chromatids to move toward opposite poles.

rows.label: Final meiotic stage with nuclear envelopes around daughter sets
rows.explanation: Telophase II encloses chromosome sets; subsequent cytokinesis completes four haploid products.

rows.label: Chromosome number per meiotic product when parent has 2n = 24
rows.explanation: Meiosis halves chromosome number, so each product receives n = 12.

rows.label: Chromosome number per mitotic daughter when parent has 2n = 24
rows.explanation: Equational mitosis preserves the parent's chromosome number in each daughter.

rows.label: DNA amount per completed meiotic product if premeiotic G1 is 2C
rows.explanation: A 2C parent first replicates to 4C, then two divisions partition it into four haploid products, each with C DNA.

rows.label: Evolutionary contribution of meiosis highlighted in the chapter
wrong: Production of only identical diploid clones
rows.explanation: Meiosis increases variation and, with fertilisation, conserves the species chromosome number across generations.

rows.label: Chlorophyll a
rows.correct: chief pigment in the reaction centre
rows.explanation: Chlorophyll a directly participates in the light reaction.

rows.label: Chlorophyll b
rows.explanation: It broadens the range of light absorbed and transfers energy to chlorophyll a.

rows.label: Photosystem II
rows.explanation: PSII absorbs best near 680 nm and begins non-cyclic electron flow.

rows.label: Photosystem I
rows.explanation: PSI absorbs best near 700 nm and reduces NADP positive.

rows.label: Photolysis of water
rows.correct: occurs on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane
rows.explanation: Water splitting supplies electrons, protons and oxygen.

rows.label: Non-cyclic photophosphorylation
rows.explanation: Both photosystems operate and electrons do not return to the source.

rows.label: Cyclic photophosphorylation
rows.correct: produces ATP but not NADPH or oxygen
rows.explanation: Only PSI participates and electrons cycle back.

rows.label: Chemiosmosis
rows.correct: ATP synthesis driven by a proton gradient
rows.explanation: Protons move through ATP synthase from lumen to stroma.

rows.label: Calvin-cycle carboxylation
rows.explanation: RuBisCO catalyses the first step of the C3 cycle.

rows.label: First stable C3 product
rows.explanation: Two molecules of 3-PGA arise after fixation of one carbon dioxide.

rows.label: Calvin-cycle reduction
rows.explanation: ATP and NADPH from the light reaction are consumed.

rows.label: RuBP regeneration
rows.explanation: Regeneration allows the Calvin cycle to continue accepting carbon dioxide.

rows.label: First stable C4 product
rows.explanation: PEP carboxylase fixes bicarbonate in mesophyll cells to form OAA.

rows.label: Kranz anatomy
rows.correct: prominent bundle-sheath cells around vascular bundles
rows.explanation: This spatial arrangement separates initial fixation from the Calvin cycle.

rows.label: PEP carboxylase
rows.correct: primary carbon dioxide-fixing enzyme in C4 mesophyll
rows.explanation: It has a high affinity for bicarbonate and lacks oxygenase activity.

rows.label: Photorespiration
rows.explanation: The pathway consumes energy and releases carbon dioxide without producing ATP.

rows.label: C4 advantage
rows.explanation: Carbon dioxide is concentrated in bundle-sheath cells.

rows.label: Blackman's law
rows.correct: rate is limited by the factor nearest its minimum
rows.explanation: Increasing a non-limiting factor does not raise photosynthetic rate.

rows.label: Light compensation point
rows.explanation: Net gas exchange is zero at this light intensity.

rows.label: Red and blue light
rows.explanation: The action spectrum broadly follows absorption by photosynthetic pigments.

rows.label: Glycolysis
rows.correct: conversion of glucose to pyruvate in the cytoplasm
rows.explanation: The EMP pathway does not require mitochondrial enzymes.

rows.label: Glycolytic investment phase
rows.explanation: ATP phosphorylates intermediates before energy payoff.

rows.label: Glycolytic net gain
rows.correct: two ATP and two NADH per glucose
rows.explanation: Four ATP are formed but two were invested.

rows.label: Pyruvate in aerobic cells
rows.explanation: It is converted to acetyl coenzyme A before the TCA cycle.

rows.label: Oxidative decarboxylation
rows.explanation: Carbon dioxide and NADH are produced by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

rows.label: Krebs cycle location
rows.explanation: Most TCA-cycle enzymes occur in the matrix.

rows.label: Acetyl coenzyme A
rows.correct: two-carbon entry molecule of the Krebs cycle
rows.explanation: It condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate.

rows.label: Substrate-level phosphorylation
rows.correct: direct enzymatic formation of ATP or GTP
rows.explanation: It occurs in glycolysis and at one step of the Krebs cycle.

rows.label: Electron transport system
rows.correct: located on the inner mitochondrial membrane
rows.explanation: Carriers pass electrons and pump protons into the intermembrane space.

rows.label: Terminal electron acceptor
rows.explanation: Oxygen combines with electrons and protons to form water.

rows.label: Oxidative phosphorylation
rows.correct: ATP formation coupled to electron transport
rows.explanation: The proton-motive force drives ATP synthase.

rows.label: Alcoholic fermentation
rows.explanation: Yeast regenerates NAD positive under anaerobic conditions.

rows.label: Lactic acid fermentation
rows.correct: forms lactate without carbon dioxide release
rows.explanation: It may occur in muscle when oxygen supply is inadequate.

rows.label: Respiratory quotient
rows.correct: carbon dioxide released divided by oxygen consumed
rows.explanation: RQ helps indicate the respiratory substrate.

rows.label: Carbohydrate RQ
rows.explanation: Equal volumes of carbon dioxide and oxygen are involved in complete glucose oxidation.

rows.label: Fat RQ
rows.explanation: Fats require proportionally more oxygen for oxidation.

rows.label: Organic-acid RQ
rows.explanation: Oxygen-rich substrates need relatively less external oxygen.

rows.label: Amphibolic pathway
rows.explanation: Respiratory intermediates are used to build cellular compounds.

rows.label: Respiratory balance sheet
rows.correct: theoretical ATP yield exceeds actual cellular yield
rows.explanation: Transport costs, leaks and alternative pathways reduce the realised total.

rows.label: Succinate dehydrogenase
rows.correct: Krebs-cycle enzyme embedded in the inner membrane
rows.explanation: It also functions as complex II of the electron transport chain.

rows.label: Growth
rows.explanation: Plant growth commonly involves cell division and enlargement.

rows.label: Open growth
rows.correct: continued production of new cells by meristems
rows.explanation: Plants retain meristematic regions throughout life.

rows.label: Arithmetic growth
rows.correct: one daughter cell continues to divide
rows.explanation: Length increases at a constant linear rate.

rows.label: Geometric growth
rows.correct: both daughter cells continue to divide
rows.explanation: Growth is exponential when resources are unlimited.

rows.label: Sigmoid growth curve
rows.explanation: Resource limitation produces the typical S-shaped curve.

rows.label: Absolute growth rate
rows.explanation: It compares actual increases in size.

rows.label: Relative growth rate
rows.correct: growth per unit initial size per time
rows.explanation: It compares efficiency relative to starting size.

rows.label: Differentiation
rows.explanation: Cells acquire structural and functional specialisation.

rows.label: Dedifferentiation
rows.correct: mature cells regain capacity to divide
rows.explanation: Interfascicular cambium can arise by dedifferentiation.

rows.label: Redifferentiation
rows.explanation: Secondary tissues produced by cambium later mature.

rows.label: Development
rows.explanation: Intrinsic and environmental factors both shape plant development.

rows.label: Plasticity
rows.correct: different structures develop in response to phase or environment
rows.explanation: Heterophylly is a common example.

rows.label: Auxin
rows.correct: promotes cell elongation and apical dominance
rows.explanation: Auxin also supports rooting and tropic responses.

rows.label: Gibberellin
rows.explanation: It can break dormancy and aid malting.

rows.label: Cytokinin
rows.correct: promotes cell division and delays senescence
rows.explanation: It helps mobilise nutrients and stimulates lateral buds.

rows.label: Ethylene
rows.explanation: It also promotes senescence and the triple response.

rows.label: Abscisic acid
rows.explanation: ABA generally inhibits growth and supports dormancy.

rows.label: Photoperiodism
rows.correct: flowering response to relative day and night length
rows.explanation: Leaves perceive the photoperiodic signal.

rows.label: Vernalisation
rows.explanation: It shortens the vegetative phase in some plants.

rows.label: Apical dominance
rows.correct: suppression of lateral buds by the shoot apex
rows.explanation: Removing the apex or applying cytokinin can release lateral buds.

rows.label: Inspiration
rows.correct: active enlargement of the thoracic chamber
rows.explanation: Contraction of diaphragm and external intercostals lowers intrapulmonary pressure.

rows.label: Expiration at rest
rows.explanation: Relaxation reduces thoracic volume and raises intrapulmonary pressure.

rows.label: Tidal volume
rows.correct: air inspired or expired in a normal breath
rows.explanation: A healthy adult exchanges about 500 mL per quiet breath.

rows.label: Inspiratory reserve volume
rows.correct: additional air inspired after a normal inspiration
rows.explanation: It is larger than tidal volume.

rows.label: Expiratory reserve volume
rows.correct: additional air expired after a normal expiration
rows.explanation: It is measured by spirometry.

rows.label: Residual volume
rows.explanation: It prevents complete lung collapse and cannot be expelled voluntarily.

rows.label: Vital capacity
rows.correct: IRV plus tidal volume plus ERV
rows.explanation: It is the maximum air expelled after a maximum inspiration.

rows.label: Total lung capacity
rows.explanation: It is the volume in lungs after maximal inspiration.

rows.label: Alveolar diffusion
rows.explanation: Thin respiratory membrane and large surface area aid exchange.

rows.label: Oxygen transport
rows.explanation: Only a small fraction travels dissolved in plasma.

rows.label: Oxygen dissociation curve
rows.correct: sigmoid relationship between oxygen pressure and saturation
rows.explanation: Cooperative binding gives haemoglobin its S-shaped curve.

rows.label: Bohr effect
rows.correct: higher carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions favour oxygen unloading
rows.explanation: Active tissues shift the curve to the right.

rows.label: Carbon dioxide transport
rows.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase in erythrocytes accelerates bicarbonate formation.

rows.label: Carbaminohaemoglobin
rows.correct: carbon dioxide bound to globin chains
rows.explanation: It accounts for part of carbon dioxide carriage.

rows.label: Chloride shift
rows.correct: chloride enters RBCs as bicarbonate leaves
rows.explanation: It maintains electrical neutrality during carbon dioxide transport.

rows.label: Medullary respiratory rhythm centre
rows.explanation: Neural groups in the medulla set the respiratory pattern.

rows.label: Chemosensitive area
rows.correct: responds strongly to carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions
rows.explanation: It modifies respiratory rhythm when these rise.

rows.label: Asthma
rows.correct: allergic inflammation and narrowing of bronchi
rows.explanation: Wheezing and difficult breathing result from airway constriction.

rows.label: Emphysema
rows.explanation: Loss of respiratory surface commonly follows chronic smoking.

rows.label: Occupational respiratory disorder
rows.correct: long exposure to dust causes inflammation and fibrosis
rows.explanation: Silica or asbestos exposure can reduce lung capacity.

rows.label: Plasma
rows.explanation: It carries proteins, nutrients, hormones and wastes.

rows.label: Erythrocytes
rows.explanation: Mammalian RBCs lack nuclei at maturity and contain haemoglobin.

rows.label: Neutrophils
rows.explanation: They engulf invading microbes.

rows.label: Lymphocytes
rows.explanation: B and T lymphocytes mediate adaptive immunity.

rows.label: Platelets
rows.explanation: They release factors that initiate coagulation.

rows.label: ABO blood groups
rows.correct: determined by A and B antigens on RBCs
rows.explanation: Naturally occurring plasma antibodies react with absent antigens.

rows.label: Rh incompatibility
rows.explanation: Anti-Rh antibodies from an Rh-negative mother may affect a later Rh-positive foetus.

rows.label: Lymph
rows.correct: tissue fluid returned through lymphatic vessels
rows.explanation: It transports absorbed fats and recirculates immune cells.

rows.label: Sinoatrial node
rows.explanation: It initiates each heartbeat in the right atrium.

rows.label: Atrioventricular node
rows.explanation: The delay permits ventricular filling before contraction.

rows.label: Cardiac cycle
rows.explanation: At about 75 beats per minute one cycle lasts roughly 0.8 second.

rows.label: Ventricular systole
rows.correct: AV valves close and semilunar valves open
rows.explanation: Rising ventricular pressure ejects blood into arteries.

rows.label: Heart sounds
rows.correct: lub and dub arise mainly from valve closure
rows.explanation: The first follows AV-valve closure and the second semilunar-valve closure.

rows.label: Cardiac output
rows.correct: heart rate multiplied by stroke volume
rows.explanation: It is about five litres per minute in a resting adult.

rows.label: Electrocardiogram P wave
rows.explanation: It precedes atrial contraction.

rows.label: Electrocardiogram QRS complex
rows.explanation: Atrial repolarisation is masked within it.

rows.label: Electrocardiogram T wave
rows.explanation: It marks electrical recovery of ventricles.

rows.label: Double circulation
rows.correct: blood passes through the heart twice per circuit
rows.explanation: Pulmonary and systemic circuits keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.

rows.label: Hepatic portal system
rows.correct: carries gut blood to the liver
rows.explanation: Absorbed nutrients first pass through hepatic capillaries.

rows.label: Hypertension
rows.correct: persistent arterial pressure above the normal range
rows.explanation: It increases risk of vascular and cardiac damage.

rows.label: Ammonotelism
rows.explanation: Aquatic animals can dilute highly toxic ammonia with abundant water.

rows.label: Ureotelism
rows.explanation: Mammals and adult amphibians convert ammonia to less toxic urea.

rows.label: Uricotelism
rows.explanation: Birds, reptiles and insects conserve water by excreting a paste.

rows.label: Kidney cortex
rows.explanation: Convoluted tubules also occur mainly in the cortex.

rows.label: Kidney medulla
rows.correct: inner region organised into renal pyramids
rows.explanation: Loops of Henle and collecting ducts extend through it.

rows.label: Nephron
rows.correct: structural and functional unit of the kidney
rows.explanation: Each includes a renal corpuscle and tubule.

rows.label: Glomerular filtration
rows.explanation: Cells and most plasma proteins remain in blood.

rows.label: Glomerular filtration rate
rows.correct: filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute
rows.explanation: A healthy adult forms about 125 mL per minute.

rows.label: Proximal convoluted tubule
rows.explanation: All glucose and amino acids and most salts and water are reclaimed normally.

rows.label: Loop of Henle
rows.explanation: Its limbs have different water and salt permeabilities.

rows.label: Counter-current mechanism
rows.correct: interaction of Henle's loop and vasa recta
rows.explanation: It helps concentrate urine while preserving the medullary gradient.

rows.label: Distal convoluted tubule
rows.explanation: Hormones adjust sodium, water and ion handling here.

rows.label: Collecting duct
rows.explanation: It passes through hyperosmotic medulla and responds to ADH.

rows.label: Antidiuretic hormone
rows.correct: increases water permeability of distal nephron
rows.explanation: ADH reduces urine volume when body water is low.

rows.label: Renin-angiotensin mechanism
rows.correct: raises pressure and promotes sodium retention
rows.explanation: Reduced renal perfusion stimulates renin release.

rows.label: Aldosterone
rows.correct: increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
rows.explanation: It acts mainly on distal tubules and collecting ducts.

rows.label: Atrial natriuretic factor
rows.correct: promotes sodium loss and lowers blood pressure
rows.explanation: It opposes renin-angiotensin-aldosterone effects.

rows.label: Micturition reflex
rows.explanation: Stretch receptors initiate a spinal reflex modified by higher centres.

rows.label: Haemodialysis
rows.correct: removes wastes across a semipermeable membrane
rows.explanation: It substitutes for renal filtration in severe kidney failure.

rows.label: Uremia
rows.correct: accumulation of urea and other wastes in blood
rows.explanation: It indicates serious loss of renal excretory function.

rows.label: Amoeboid movement
rows.explanation: Macrophages and leucocytes can move this way.

rows.label: Ciliary movement
rows.explanation: It moves ova in oviducts and mucus in airways.

rows.label: Muscular movement
rows.explanation: Interaction of actin and myosin generates force.

rows.label: Sarcomere
rows.correct: segment between two successive Z lines
rows.explanation: It is the functional contractile unit of striated muscle.

rows.label: Thin filament
rows.correct: mainly actin with troponin and tropomyosin
rows.explanation: Its regulatory proteins control access to myosin-binding sites.

rows.label: Thick filament
rows.explanation: Projecting heads bind actin and hydrolyse ATP.

rows.label: Sliding-filament theory
rows.correct: thin filaments slide over thick filaments
rows.explanation: Filament lengths remain constant as the sarcomere shortens.

rows.label: Calcium in contraction
rows.explanation: This moves tropomyosin away from actin's active sites.

rows.label: ATP in contraction
rows.explanation: Fresh ATP allows myosin to release actin.

rows.label: A band
rows.explanation: It corresponds to the full length of thick filaments.

rows.label: I band
rows.explanation: It contains regions with thin filaments only.

rows.label: H zone
rows.explanation: Thin filaments slide into the central thick-filament region.

rows.label: Axial skeleton
rows.correct: skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum
rows.explanation: It forms the central supporting axis.

rows.label: Appendicular skeleton
rows.explanation: Pectoral and pelvic girdles attach limbs to the axial skeleton.

rows.label: Ball-and-socket joint
rows.explanation: Shoulder and hip are examples.

rows.label: Hinge joint
rows.correct: mainly permits movement in one plane
rows.explanation: Elbow and knee are examples.

rows.label: Pivot joint
rows.explanation: The atlas-axis articulation enables head rotation.

rows.label: Myasthenia gravis
rows.explanation: Antibodies impair transmission to skeletal muscle.

rows.label: Muscular dystrophy
rows.explanation: Muscle fibres weaken over time.

rows.label: Gout
rows.explanation: Elevated uric acid can cause painful inflammation.

rows.label: Central nervous system
rows.explanation: It integrates sensory input and coordinates responses.

rows.label: Peripheral nervous system
rows.correct: nerves connecting CNS with the body
rows.explanation: Cranial and spinal nerves carry afferent and efferent signals.

rows.label: Somatic neural system
rows.explanation: It also carries conscious sensory information.

rows.label: Autonomic neural system
rows.explanation: Sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions often have opposing effects.

rows.label: Neuron
rows.correct: structural and functional unit of neural tissue
rows.explanation: Dendrites receive signals and the axon conducts impulses away.

rows.label: Myelin sheath
rows.explanation: It permits rapid saltatory conduction.

rows.label: Node of Ranvier
rows.explanation: Action potentials are regenerated at these nodes.

rows.label: Resting membrane potential
rows.correct: inside of neuron is negative relative to outside
rows.explanation: Selective permeability and ion pumps maintain ionic gradients.

rows.label: Depolarisation
rows.correct: rapid sodium entry makes membrane potential less negative
rows.explanation: Voltage-gated sodium channels open after threshold is reached.

rows.label: Repolarisation
rows.explanation: Voltage-gated potassium channels dominate this phase.

rows.label: Action potential
rows.explanation: Its size does not increase with a stronger suprathreshold stimulus.

rows.label: Saltatory conduction
rows.correct: impulse appears to jump node to node
rows.explanation: It is faster and more energy-efficient in myelinated fibres.

rows.label: Electrical synapse
rows.correct: ions pass directly through gap junctions
rows.explanation: Transmission is very rapid and usually bidirectional.

rows.label: Chemical synapse
rows.explanation: Transmission has a short delay and is usually unidirectional.

rows.label: Neurotransmitter release
rows.correct: triggered by calcium entry into the presynaptic terminal
rows.explanation: Synaptic vesicles fuse with the membrane by exocytosis.

rows.label: Reflex action
rows.correct: rapid involuntary response to a stimulus
rows.explanation: A reflex arc can operate through the spinal cord.

rows.label: Sensory neuron
rows.explanation: It forms the afferent limb of a reflex arc.

rows.label: Motor neuron
rows.correct: carries impulses from CNS to an effector
rows.explanation: It forms the efferent limb of a reflex arc.

rows.label: Interneuron
rows.explanation: It integrates information between sensory and motor pathways.

rows.label: Threshold stimulus
rows.correct: minimum stimulus that triggers an action potential
rows.explanation: Subthreshold depolarisation does not generate a propagated impulse.

rows.label: Hypothalamus
